                                   Direct Testimony of Jeffry Pollock


                                           Executive Summary


             Real Time Pricing was an innovative cost-based rate that was very beneficial for both

 2   Georgia Power Company and its' customers when it was introduced in 1992.               It allowed the

 3   customers a means to moderate standard industrial tariffs, which are uncompetitive with

 4   surrounding states, so that the customer's total blended cost would remain competitive. The rate

 5   gave Georgia Power Company a powerful tool to compete for new industry with rates substantially

 6   less than the regular standard tariff rates charged to its existing customers.

 7          As Georgia Power Company's capacity reserves decreased during the 90's, the RTP load

 8   was served by increasingly expensive native generation and, most significantly, purchase power.

 9   This included spot purchases, which are exceedingly expensive and will remain so until the

10   deregulated wholesale markets mature and sufficient merchant capacity is attracted to Georgia to

11   serve available customers. While "hot summers" have been blamed for escalating RTP prices in

12   the past two years, the price increases and volatility are more attributable to Georgia Power

13   Company's apparent unwillingness to protect its captive customers from the extreme high prices


                                                      -i-
                                                                                      Executive Summary
                                           BRUBAKER & AsSOCIATES, INC.


                                                                                                 It   h

                                                                                             STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment C


     and volatility caused by tight capacity supplies and price-deregulated wholesale markets. Under

 2   this scenario, the flaws and inequities of the existing tariff structure have become pronounced with

 3   the result that RTP prices have increased at an average of almost 7% a year since 1992. Because

 4   of these changing circumstances, RTP is no longer a cost-based rate.

 5          The GTMA/GIG Peti.tion and this testimony identify the specific ways that the tariffs can be

 6   modified to restore the cost basis and to more equitably balance the risks until a more permanent

 7   cost-based option of purchasing electricity can be allowed to industrial customers. These areas of

 8   adjustment are as follows:

 9          •       First, remove the risk adder of 0.5¢ per kWh (0.45¢ for RTP-HA). As the
10                  RTP tariffs are applied by GPC, the Company has no risk. All risk has been
11                  shifted to the customer. The margins from RTP sales are excessive and
12                  unreasonable. Removing the adder will restore the margins to a more
13                  reasonable level that more clearly reflects the cost to provide the service.

14                  Second, require GPC to properly administer the RTP tariffs or implement
15                  "lambda averaging." The RTP tariffs do not allow purchased power costs to
16                  be included in the hourly price, contrary to actual practice. This practice
17                  should cease immediately. Alternatively, the price should be based on the
18                  average cost of the native and purchased energy resources used to supply
19                  RTP (i.e., lambda averaging) so that it reflects the actual cost of the power.
20                  GPC prices RTP at the cost of the last and most expensive resource
21                  employed.     This practice is tantamount to selling a lot full of Ford
22                  automobiles at a Mercedes price just because one Mercedes happens to be
23                  parked on the same lot.

24          •       Third, modify the fuel accounting to reflect the actual real time cost of the
25                  generated or purchased energy used to set the hourly prices.            This
26                  practice will avoid an artificial underrecovery of fuel under the Georgia
27                  Power interpretation. Any underrecovery is separately and additionally
28                  recovered from all customers.

29          •      Fourth, require accountability by Georgia Power Company to its
30                 customers for its purchasing practices. The design of the RTP rate offers
31                 no incentive to GPC to purchase energy for the least dollar cost and the
32                 customers presently have no right to seek lower cost suppliers of
33                 electricity.
34          These changes can be made without reopening or violating the terms of the Accounting

35   Order approved in GPC's last rate case, Docket No. 9355-U. The Accounting Order cannot and

36   should not be used as an excuse to deny the Petition, to make only a temporary fix in the rate or

     wait until the next rate case before implementing the changes necessary to make RTP fair, just and

 2   reasonable.

 3           The next rate case, which cannot give effective relief until January 2002, is an

 4   unrealistically long delay to businesses whose performance is judged on a quarterly basis.           In

 5   today's fast-moving and changing business climate, survival goes to those companies that can

 6   minimize their costs, including the cost of electricity. Electricity is a significant operating cost of

 7   GTMA and GIG members. Competitive electricity prices are essential to the economic well-being

 8   of these customers and the State of Georgia.

 9           The changes to RTP that are described in the testimony are designed to restore the

1O   competitiveness that has been lost due to the drastic price increases. Further, they will make RTP

11   a rate that is fair, just and reasonable.

                                II. Why the Petition Was Filed


     Q   WHY DID GTMA AND GIG FILE THE PETITION FOR RULE NISI?

 2   A   The GTMA/GIG Petition was filed to address serious problems with GPC's RTP tariffs.

 3       These serious problems include:

 4       1.     Concerns about the overall competitiveness of GPC's rates in light of recent
 5              drastic increases in average RTP prices;

 6       2.     The RTP tariffs are not being properly applied because purchased power costs
 7              are included in the hourly running cost of incremental generation; and

 8       3.     Dramatic changes in circumstances since the inception of RTP have resulted in
 9              prices that are no longer fair, just and reasonable and which are providing
10              excessive revenues to GPC.           As explained below, certain of the design
11              parameters of the RTP tariffs need to be updated in order to bring the rate more
12              in line with cost and to mitigate the excess revenues being enjoyed by GPC at its
13              customers' expense.


14   Q   WHY IS IT NECESSARY FOR GPC TO OFFER RTP?

15   A   GPC's standard rates are more expensive than the corresponding standard rates of

16       other utilities in the southeastern United States. This is shown in Exhibit _ _ (JP-1 ).

17       As can be seen from this Exhibit, all three comparisons demonstrate that GPC's

18       standard industrial tariff is priced well-above the average rate for similar service offered

19       by investor-owned utilities (IOU) in the Southeast.        For example, page 1 shows that,

20       based on industrial rates in effect on July 1, 1998, GPC ranked 15th out of 40

21       southeastern IOUs. (A ranking of 1 is the most expensive, and a ranking of 40 is the

22       least expensive.)   By July 1. 1999 (page 2), GPC ranked 14th most expensive.          This

23       means that 25 and 26 other Southeastern IOUs priced their standard industrial service

24       below GPC, respectively in 1998 and 1999.

                 The rankings shown on pages 1 and 2 were developed from various Edison

 2       Electric Institute (EEi) publications for an industrial customer having a 68% monthly load

 3       factor, which is consistent with EEi's assumptions.


 4   Q   DO GPC'S STANDARD RATES COMPARE MORE FAVORABLY FOR HIGHER LOAD

 5       FACTOR CUSTOMERS?

 6   A   No. Exhibit __ (JP-1 ), page 3, shows the results of a BAI survey of rates in effect on

 7       January 1, 2000 for 90% load factor customers. Further, unlike the prior EEi surveys,

 8       BAl's Southeastern Survey includes a major competitor to GPC, the Tennessee Valley

 9       Authority (TVA).

1O               The BAI survey confirms that GPC's standard industrial tariffs are priced above

11       the average.       Specifically, GPC is the 10th most expensive out of 33 utilities in the

12       survey. This means that 23 other utilities, including TVA, charged less for industrial high

13       load factor service than GPC.


14   Q   HOW IS RTP USED IN CONJUNCTION WITH GPC'S STANDARD TARIFFS?

15   A   The standard tariffs apply to a customer's existing load prior to commencing RTP

16       service. This existing load is referred to as a customer baseline load (or CSL). RTP

17       applies to a customer's actual hourly loads when those loads differ from the CSL.

18               For example, if a customer's hourly load is above the CSL, the customer is

19       charged the hourly real time price. Similarly, if a customer's hourly load is below the

20       CBL, the customer is paid the hourly real time price. If a customer continues to operate

21       at the CBL, then the customer would continue to pay the same total cost as under the

22       standard tariff.

23               Thus, customers that operate above the CBL during low-cost hours and/or below

24       the CBL in high-cost hours will reduce their average cost of electricity. The net result of

             using RTP is that the total blended cost of electricity can be more competitive than the

 2           standard firm rates.


 3   Q       HOW HAS THE RTP RATE HISTORICALLY HELPED TO MAKE GPC'S RATES

 4           MORE COMPETITIVE?

 5   A       RTP has historically been used in conjunction with a standard tariff to allow customers to

 6           reduce their average cost of electricity.

 7                   RTP was designed to be a cost-based rate option designed to reflect GPC's

 8           incremental cost of generation and transmission. The standard tariffs, by contrast, are

 9           designed to fully recover GPC's embedded cost, which include generation, transmission,

1O           distribution and other overhead costs. Because the incremental cost of generation and

11           transmission is below GPC's overall embedded cost of service, RTP service costs less

12           than taking service under GPC's standard tariffs. As explained later, RTP is no longer a

13           cost-based rate and it is no longer providing a competitive advantage for GPC

14           customers.


15   Q       DOES GPC OFFER DIFFERENT TYPES OF REAL TIME PRICING SERVICE?

16   A       Yes.   GPC offers two RTP options:          Day-Ahead (DA) and Hour-Ahead (HA).              The

17           RTP-DA and RTP-HA tariffs are similar in structure.              Both require the customer to

18          establish a CBL, and the hourly prices include the running cost of incremental
                                                                    1
19           generation, losses and a recovery factor or adder.         As discussed later, the adder is a flat

20           charge per kilowatthour (kWh) and it provides a contribution to fixed costs (i.e., profit).

21           Under certain circumstances, the hourly prices will include an outage factor and a charge


             1
              Losses are added to the incremental generation cost because this cost is initially quoted at the
     power plant, and some energy is consumed to deliver electricity from the generator to a customer.

                                                                                               Page 6


         for incremental transmission. However, the running cost of incremental generation, or

 2       system lambda, is by far the most significant component of the hourly real time prices.


 3   Q   WHAT ARE THE KEY DIFFERENCES BETWEEN RTP-DA AND RTP-HA?

 4   A   There are two key differences. First, for RTP-DA customers, GPC determines by 4:00

 5       p.m. the 24 hourly prices applicable on the next day. This is in contrast to HA service

 6       where the price for each hour is not determined until one-hour before service

 7       commences.

 8              Second, the two RTP options have different adders. The DA adder is 0.5¢ per

 9       kWh, while the corresponding HA adder is 0.45¢ per kWh.


10   Q   HOW MUCH LOAD IS PRICED ON RTP VS. THE STANDARD TARIFFS?

11   A   RTP sales account for about 34% of the total energy sold to RTP customers.             The

12       remaining 66% is priced under a standard tariff.


13   Q   DO THE LOWER PRICES OFFERED BY RTP COME FREELY WITH NO RISK?

14   A   No.   Unlike any other retail customer served by GPC, RTP customers experience

15       immediate price level changes as a result of projected changes in the hourly running

16       cost of generation and purchased power.

17              For example, if GPC projects a need to purchase power on the wholesale spot

18       market at a cost of $6 per kWh, the same $6 per kWh cost, plus additional markups, will

19       be immediately reflected in the hourly RTP. If GPC does not effectively control these

20       costs, then it jeopardizes the competitiveness of the RTP program. This, in turn, further

21       jeopardizes the competitiveness of the customers that have come to rely upon RTP as a

22       way to keep jobs in Georgia.

                There are also circumstances in which a customer cannot respond to higher

 4       workers go and/or losing sales to a competitor.

     Q   IS PRICE VOLATILITY THE MAJOR ISSUE?

 2   A   No.     Price level is more important than volatility to GTMA and GIG members.

 3       Average RTP prices have increased drastically during the summers of 1998 and 1999.

 4       Since 1997, average RTP prices have increased by over 1¢ per kWh, a 44% increase.

 5       This translates into a 13% overall price increase to an average RTP customer. These

 6       drastic increases in RTP prices are in stark contrast to GPC's other rates, which have

 7       dropped since 1997. This is primarily due to the base rate reduction implemented in

 8       GPC's last rate case.


 9   Q   WHAT HAS BEEN THE LONG-TERM TREND IN THE GPC'S ELECTRICITY PRICES?

10   A   The long-term trend is shown in Exhibit _ _ (JP-2). This Exhibit shows the year-to-year

11       percentage change in average RTP prices with the corresponding prices charged to

12       residential, small business and large business customers. As clearly shown in this chart,

13       RTP-DA prices have increased on average by 7.1% per year. During this same period,

14       all other non-RTP prices decreased annually by between 0.6% and 1.9%.

15                Thus, RTP is the only tariff to have experienced price increases over the long-

16       term.


17   Q   WHAT FACTORS ARE CAUSING THE HIGHER PRICES UNDER THE RTP TARIFFS?

18   A   The higher average RTPs can be attributed primarily to two factors.       First, GPC has

19       improperly included purchased power costs in determining the hourly price.       Second,

20       circumstances have changed dramatically since RTP was first implemented as a pilot

21       program in 1993.


                                                                    II. Why the Petition Was Filed

                                      BRUBAKER & AsSOCIATES, INC.

     Q   WHY DO YOU CONTEND THAT GPC HAS IMPROPERLY INCLUDED PURCHASED

 2       POWER COSTS IN DETERMINING THE HOURLY PRICES?

 3   A   The approved RTP tariffs state that "the hourly prices are based on projections of the

 4       hourly running cost of incremental generation." (emphasis added) However, generation

 5       is not functionally equivalent to purchased power.            Generation means electricity

 6       produced by a utility from power plants that the utility owns.         Purchased power, by

 7       contrast, refers to electricity purchased by a utility from resources that are owned by a

 8       third party - either a utility, a marketer or a non-utility generator (NUG).


 9   Q   IS THERE ALSO A DISTINCTION BETWEEN GENERATION AND PURCHASED

10       POWER IN GENERALLY ACCEPTED ACCOUNTING PRACTICE?

11   A   Yes.   The FERC System of Accounts also distinguishes between generation-related

12       expenses and purchased power. Specifically, generation:related expenses are booked

13       to Accounts 500 through 554.        Purchased power costs, by contrast, are booked to

14       Account 555.


15   Q   DOES THIS COMMISSION RECOGNIZE THAT GENERATION AND PURCHASED

16       POWER ARE NOT FUNCTIONALLY EQUIVALENT?

17   A   Yes.   GPC's FCR tariff distinguishes between the cost of energy generated and the

18       energy cost of purchased power. If generation and purchased power were the same,

19       then there would have been no need for a separate reference to purchased power.


                                                                     II. Why the Petition Was Filed

                                       BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.


                                                                                                           11

                                                                                           STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment C


                                                                                          Jeffry Pollock
                                                                                                Page 10


     Q      WAS THERE ANY INDICATION THAT GPC                          HAD INTENDED TO INCLUDE

 2          PURCHASED POWER IN THE HOURLY REAL TIME PRICES WHEN RTP WAS

 3          FIRST IMPLEMENTED?

 4   A      No.   The testimony sponsored by GPC witnesses in 1992 made no mention that

 5          purchased power cost would be included in determining the hourly running cost of

 6          incremental generation, or system lambda. Specifically, the term system lambda was

 7          used synonymously with incremental plant operating costs. 2 This same testimony goes

 8          on to state that "the magnitude of this cost [incremental plant operating cost] will vary

 9          with the hourly mix of generation resources that are then in use for meeting Georgia

10          Power Company's territorial load." 3


11   Q      WHY ELSE IS INCLUDING PURCHASED POWER IN DETERMINING THE HOURLY

12          RTPs NOT APPROPRIATE?

13   A      Wholesale power markets have changed dramatically since the inception of RTP in

14          Georgia.    The Energy Policy Act of 1992 gave the Federal Energy Regulatory

15          Commission (FERC) authority to require all utilities under its jurisdiction to provide open

16          nondiscriminatory access to the transmission system. The FERC subsequently issued

17          Order No. 888 in April 1996. The effect of Order No. 888 has been a dramatic increase

18         in the use of transmission services by third parties. This, in turn, has reduced the vertical

19          market power of transmission-owning utilities. The FERC has granted authority to allow

20         utilities and other wholesale market participants to buy and sell electricity at market-

21         based prices. This, coupled with the movement to customer choice by 24 states, has

22         resulted in a wholesale market that today is, for all intents and purposes, price

23         deregulated.

            2
              Testimony of Jonathan M. Kubler and Michael T. O'Sheasy on behalf of Georgia Power
     Compan:f.', Docket No. 4147-U, May 11, 1992, page 10. (emphasis added)
              Id. (emphasis added)


                                                                        II. Why the Petition Was Filed

                                         BRUBAKER & AsSOCIATES, INC.

                                                                                                   STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment C


                                                                                               Jeffry Pollock
                                                                                                       Page 11


                    By including spot wholesale purchases in the hourly RTPs, GPC's captive

 2       customers are now being exposed to more price risk than ever before.                       As stated

 3       previously, a projected market-based purchased power transaction, as high as $6 per

 4       kWh in 1999, will immediately be reflected in the hourly price. No other retail customer

 5       will immediately see this $6 per kWh price. 4 If the power is actually purchased, then the

 6       cost will be charged to the fuel account and passed through to all customers.                      This

 7       automatic pass-through of actual fuel and purchased energy costs demonstrates that

 8       GPC bears absolutely no risk to provide RTP service.

 9                  Although RTP is a regulated service, the hourly prices are increasingly being

10       influenced by the deregulated wholesale market. Fairness demands that if a regulated

11       tariff allows the pass-through of deregulated prices, then the captive customers should

12       have more options than simply reducing load to offset the higher prices.                   The most

13       effective option is to allow the customer to choose an alternative supplier. However, until

14       customer choice is authorized in Georgia, the Commission must continue to function as

15       a "surrogate for competition" to ensure that regulated prices are fair, just and reasonable.


16   Q   ARE THERE ANY OTHER REASONS WHY PURCHASED POWER COSTS SHOULD

17       BE REMOVED FROM THE HOURLY PRICES?

18   A   As I shall demonstrate later, the significant increase in the hourly prices has provided a

19       windfall to GPC in terms of excess revenues collected from RTP sales.


20   Q   HOW        HAVE     CHANGING        CIRCUMSTANCES           ALSO     RESULTED        IN    DRASTIC

21       INCREASES IN REAL TIME PRICES?

22   A   RTP was implemented at a time when The Southern Company (Southern) system had

23       surplus capacity.        Most of the surplus capacity consisted of low-cost base load

         4
             $6 per kWh is about 80 times the average cost to serve a residential customer.

                                           BRUBAKER & AsSOCIATES, INC.

         resources.         Southern's planning reserve margins were in the 15% to 20% range.

 2       Wholesale markets were also price-regulated.

 3                   Based on these factors, the differential between marginal energy cost and

 4       embedded cost was small. Referencing GPC's testimony in Docket No. 4147-U, GPC

 5       had projected in 1992 a marginal energy cost (or system lambda) of 1.5¢ per kWh. 5 This

 6       is only slightly higher than the FCR in effect in 1992 of 1.3¢. 6

 7                   Today, however, the surplus of low-cost base load resources has been depleted.

 8       Southern has lowered its planning reserve margin to 13.5%. Capacity additions have

 9       also not kept pace with growing demand.                   Consequently, Southern has relied

10       increasingly on more expensive generation and purchased power to meet territorial load.

11                  Thus, marginal energy costs are significantly higher than embedded energy

12       costs. For example, in 1999, the average day-ahead RTP price was 3.57¢. The current

13       FCR is 1.37¢. As explained later, this fact demonstrates why the RTP adders should be

14       eliminated.


15   Q   WILL MARGINAL ENERGY COSTS EXCEED EMBEDDED COSTS FOR THE

16       FORESEEABLE FUTURE?

17   A   Yes. Southern will continue to rely on more expensive generation and purchased power

18       in order to maintain reliability. Most future resource additions will be fueled with natural

19       gas.      The operating cost of new gas-fired units will be significantly higher than the

20       corresponding cost of operating GPC's coal-fired units, even when the lower heat rate of

21       the new gas facilities is considered.

             1d., Footnote 1.

             FCR-13 raised embedded fuel costs to over 1.5¢ in late 1993.

     Adder

 2   Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE ADDER?

 3   A   The adder is a fixed amount that is charged for every RTP kWh purchased or sold. At

 4       present, the adder is 0.5¢ under RTP-DA and 0.45¢ under RTP-HA.


 5   Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THE ADDER?

 6   A   The adder was originally designed to serve two purposes.                First, it provided a

 7       contribution to fixed costs (i.e., profit).      Second, it compensated GPC for the risks

 8       associated with RTP. This is perhaps why GPC originally described the adder as a "risk

 9       recovery factor." 9


10   Q   WHY IS IT NECESSARY FOR RTP CUSTOMERS TO PROVIDE A CONTRIBUTION

11       TO FIXED COSTS?

12   A   Every rate should provide some contribution of fixed costs or profit, and RTP is no

13       exception.       If RTP sales provide some revenue to defray GPC's fixed costs, all other

14       non-RTP customers will benefit. This is because the margins generated from RTP sales

15       will lower the revenue requirement recoverable from, and the rates chargeable to, non-

16       RTP customers.


17   Q   WHAT RISKS WERE INITIALLY ATTRIBUTABLE TO RTP?

18   A   While other utilities were beginning to implement small scale experimental programs,

19       GPC was seeking Commission approval for a full-scale RTP program. At that time, RTP

20       was still a novel pricing mechanism.         GPC did not have much experience projecting

21       hourly real time prices on a day-ahead basis. There was a risk that the quoted day-

22       ahead prices would understate actual energy costs.

         9
             1d., Footnote 1.


                                                                          Ill. The Requested Relief

                                         BRUBAKER & AsSOCIATES, INC .


                                                              ... TTl    ----···--·-----·------..,.,-,-11---.--1-,-

                                                                                                 STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment C


                                                                                              Jeffry Pollock
                                                                                                    Page 17


                     Finally, GPC did not know how customers would respond to RTP. To the extent

 2           that customers' response was more than the Company had anticipated, this could

 3           produce revenue erosion. The risk recovery factor was designed to offset this erosion

 4           and the other risks associated with RTP.


 5   Q       IS AN ADDER STILL APPROPRIATE IN TODAY'S CIRCUMSTANCES?

 6   A       No. When RTP was first implemented, marginal energy costs and embedded energy

 7           costs were similar. Thus, the 0.5¢ adder was necessary to ensure that every kWh sold

 8           under RTP would provide some contribution toward fixed cost recovery or profit. Today,

 9           however, marginal energy costs are much higher than embedded energy costs. This

10           means that every kWh sold under RTP already provides some profit without the need for

11           an additional 0.5¢ (or 0.45¢) adder.


12   Q       DO OTHER UTILITIES IMPOSE A FIXED ADDER ON ALL RTP KWh SALES?

13   A      . Yes.   Some southeast utilities, like Duke Power Company and Virginia Electric and

14           Power Company, do charge a flat adder for all RTP kWh sold. Duke Power Company's

15           adder is 0.5¢, the same as GPC's RTP-DA tariff. Virginia Electric and Power Company

16           charges a 0.6¢ adder on RTP sales. However, both utilities have lower standard rates

17           than GPC. 1° Further, Duke Power's average real time prices were lower and less

18           volatile than GPC's during the summers of 1998 and 1999.

     Power rankings are 19th, 18th and 26th. These compare to GPC rankings of 15th, 14th and 10th (1 =most
     expensive).

     Q   IS A FLAT CENTS PER KWh ADDER A UNIVERSAL PRACTICE?

 2   A   No. Several southeast utilities charge a variable adder. These utilities include Carolina

 3       Power & Light Company, Central Power and Light Company, FPL and Southwestern

 4       Electric Power Company. The variable adder is stated as a percentage of the difference

 5       between the average cost per kWh under the standard tariff and the corresponding

 6       hourly marginal energy cost.

 7              For example, assume that a standard tariff has an average cost of 4¢ per kWh

 8       and the utility is allowed to retain 20% of the difference between the standard tariff and

 9       marginal energy cost.    If the marginal energy cost were 2¢, then the adder would be

10       0.4¢ per kWh (20% x (4¢ - 2¢)]. On the other hand, if marginal energy costs were above

11       4¢, then no adder would be charged. The latter circumstance is most likely to occur

12       during extreme hot weather conditions, when generation supplies are tight, and/or the

13       utility is having to purchase spot-market energy to satisfy customer demand.


14   Q   IS THE ADDER NEEDED TO PROVIDE A REASONABLE CONTRIBUTION TO GPC'S

15       FIXED COSTS, OR PROFIT?

16   A   No.   RTP sales are generating sufficient margins without the adder to provide a

17       reasonable contribution to GPC's fixed costs, or profit.

     Q   SHOULD THE ADDER BE RETAINED TO COMPENSATE FOR THE RISKS

1O       energy prices.    This is because all eligible fuel and purchased energy costs are

     Lambda Averaging
 2   Q   WHAT IS SYSTEM LAMBDA?

 3   A   System lambda is the term used to describe the hourly running cost of incremental

 4       generation.    It consists primarily of incremental fuel cost and a small amount of

 5       incremental variable operation and maintenance expense (VOM).


 6   Q   HOW DOES GPC DEFINE SYSTEM LAMBDA IN THE CONTEXT OF THE RTP

 7       TARIFFS?

 8   A   System lambda is not defined in the RTP tariffs. GPC chooses to define system lambda

 9       as the cost of the next kWh generated or purchased to serve territorial load.       This

1O       definition is illustrated in Exhibit _ _ (JP-8).

11               The illustration is a hypothetical example of a series of resources (either

12       generation or purchased power) that have been dispatched to serve 1,000 megawatts

13       (MW) of RTP load in a given hour. In this hypothetical, the resources are assumed to be

14       equal in size and range in cost from 3¢ to 7¢ per kWh.

15               Based on this hypothetical example, the system lambda employed by GPC in the

16       RTP tariffs would be 7¢ per kWh. Consequently, all RTP sales in this hour would be

17       priced to reflect the 7¢ system lambda, even though the vast majority of the kWh serving

18       RTP load would cost much less.


19   Q   WHAT IS MEANT BY THE TERM LAMBDA AVERAGING?

20   A   Lambda averaging means calculating the weighted average cost of resources operating

21       on the margin to serve a particular block of load. Using the illustration in Exhibit __

22       (JP-8), lambda averaging applied to 1,000 MW of RTP load would result in a charge of

23       only 5¢ per kWh.

     Q   WHICH APPROACH IS PREFERABLE, GPC'S OR LAMBDA AVERAGING?

 2   A   Lambda averaging is clearly the preferable approach. As can be seen in Exhibit __

 3       (JP-5), using lambda averaging to set the hourly price would reflect the actual hourly

 4       incremental cost to serve RTP load. Pricing RTP at the most expensive kWh, as GPC

 5       does, is no longer cost-based, and it results in higher costs to customers and excessive

 6       margins to GPC.


 7   Q   WHY    ELSE    IS   GPC'S    DEFINITION        OF    SYSTEM   LAMBDA     NO     LONGER

 8       APPROPRIATE?

 9   A   As discussed earlier, circumstances have changed dramatically since the initial

10       implementation of RTP. First and foremost, the size of the RTP program has increased

11       dramatically, from 370 average MW in 1995 to over 1,000 average MW in 1999.

12              Second, there is a much wider disparity in the cost of marginal resources. For

13       example, the incremental cost of generation can range from 3¢ to 3.5¢ for expensive

14       coal units to up to 7.5¢ for peaking capacity. This is in contrast to purchased power

15       costs, which have ranged in magnitude from 3.5¢ to 50¢ per kWh during the summer of

16       1998, and from 8.5¢ to $6 per kWh during the summer of 1999.

17              The widening cost disparity, coupled with the greater reliance on expensive spot

18       market purchases, has caused system lambda to exceed 10¢ per kWh on more than just

19       a few occasions in 1998 and 1999, as shown in the attached table.

        Q    WHAT IS THE IMPACT OF LAMBDA AVERAGING?

 2      A    At a minimum, lambda averaging of purchased power would reduce GPC revenues by

 3           between $7 million and $24 million per year. 12 The specific impact will vary each year

 4           depending on the amount and cost of all bottom-of-stack power purchases. GPC refused

 5           to quantify the impact of lambda averaging applied to all of the incremental resources

 6           (i.e., purchased power and generation) used to serve RTP load. Averaging the entire

 7           RTP stack would have a bigger impact than averaging only bottom-of-stack purchases.


 8     Q     WHAT ACTION SHOULD THE COMMISSION TAKE ON THE SYSTEM LAMBDA

 9           ISSUE?

10     A     For all of the above-stated reasons, the Commission should either:

11                      •       Eliminate purchased power expense from the system lambda
12                              calculation, consistent with the terms and conditions in the
13                              approved RTP tariffs; or

14                      •       Replace GPC's definition of system lambda with lambda
15                              averaging of at least the last 1,000 MW of resources (generation
16                              and purchased power) operating on the margin, similar in concept
17                              as FPL and TVA. The 1,000 MW approximates the average RTP
18                              load served by GPC.

19           Lambda averaging, as described above, will ensure that the revenues collected from

20           RTP sales more closely reflect actual incremental generation cost.


21     Fuel Accounting Practice
22     Q     WHAT IS THE PROBLEM WITH THE FUEL ACCOUNTING PRACTICE ASSOCIATED

23           WITH RTP?

24     A     GPC does not charge the appropriate amount of fuel cost recovery from RTP sales. As

25           a consequence, all customers are paying higher fuel costs. This problem is illustrated in


             12
                  GPC's response to Staff Data Request 2-1.

                                              BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.


     1-1 ITT T lf T r . T - llrrT· . . ~ -·· ..                                                             11

                                                                                     STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment C


                                                                                   Jeffry Pollock
                                                                                         Page 27


         Exhibit __ (JP-9). The illustration in this Exhibit is based on the same hypothetical

 2       example used to explain lambda averaging.

 3              In this hypothetical example, I have assumed that system lambda, as defined by

 4       GPC, would be 7.0¢.       The actual incremental fuel and VOM (or purchased power)

 5       expense is assumed to be 5.0¢. This represents the weighted average cost of all of the

 6       resources operating on the margin to serve 1,000 MW of RTP load. This 5.0¢ actual

 7       cost would go into the FCR account as an eligible expense.

 8              The problem arises because of the 5.0¢ expense added to the FCR account,

 9       GPC assumes that only average fuel costs are recoverable from RTP customers. In this

10       case, the average fuel cost, or FCR, is assumed to be 1.4¢.       Therefore, 3.6¢ (the

11       difference between actual cost of 5.0¢ and recovery of 1.4¢) becomes an uncollected

12       fuel expense.


13   Q   WHAT HAPPENS TO THE 3.6¢ OF REVENUE THAT WAS COLLECTED IN THE

14       HOURLY PRICE?

15   A   GPC deems this to be a recovery of nonfuel-related costs. Thus, the 3.6¢ provides an

16       additional margin to GPC. Based on the hypothetical illustration in Exhibit _ _ (JP-9),

17       the 7¢ system lambda, coupled with GPC's erroneous fuel accounting practice, will yield

18       a total margin of 5.6¢ (7.0¢ - 1.4¢) before the adder.


19   Q   HOW DOES THIS ACCOUNTING PRACTICE AFFECT FCR?

20   A   The FCR is designed to enable the Company to recover all of its eligible fuel and

21       purchased power costs. Thus, any under-collection of these costs, regardless of the

22       source of the under-collection, will cause the FCR to be higher than would otherwise be

23       the case.


                                                                      Ill. The Requested Relief

                                      BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.

                                                                                           STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment C


                                                                                         Jeffry Pollock
                                                                                               Page 28


       Q     IS GPC'S TREATMENT OF RTP FUEL COSTS REASONABLE?

 2     A     No. If a pricing mechanism adjusts GPC's revenues to reflect actual system operating

 3           conditions, then it is just as reasonable for a cost recovery mechanism to reflect similar

 4           real time adjustments. Using the hypothetical illustration, if GPC incurs a 5¢ fuel cost

 5           and that cost is reflected in the hourly RTP, then the corresponding fuel cost recovery

 6           should also be 5¢. In other words, the Company should deem the fuel recovery at 5¢,

 7           rather than 1.4¢.


 8     Q     HOW WOULD THIS CHANGE IN THE FUEL ACCOUNTING PRACTICE AFFECT

 g           GPC?

10     A     GPC's earnings would be reduced because a portion of the RTP base revenues would

11           be used to offset eligible fuel and purchased power costs. This would lower the FCR. A

12           lower FCR would benefit all customers.


13     Disclosure of Energy Procurement Practices
14     Q     WHY DOES THE PETITION SEEK TO ESTABLISH STANDARDS FOR GPC TO

15           DISCLOSE ITS ENERGY PROCUREMENT PRACTICES?

16     A     This is a very important element of the Petition because GPC has no real incentive to

17           minimize purchased energy costs. All purchased energy costs are recoverable in the

18           FCR. If GPC were, instead, to acquire options or to prearrange purchases in advance,

19           the cost of such options and any capacity-related costs would not be recoverable

20           through the FCR.

21                  For example, if GPC projects that purchased power will cost $6 per kWh, all of

22           this cost, plus the various markups, will be immediately reflected in the projected RTP

23           prices. Had this purchase been prearranged at a cost of only 10¢, and assuming that

24          this resource was projected to be on the margin, then the 10¢ cost would be reflected in


                                                                           Ill. The Requested Relief

                                          BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.


     I "'l ITT T lI r     r . T -·lrrT 1.. . . .. ... -·

                                                                                               STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment C


                                                                                              Jeffry Pollock
                                                                                                    Page 29


              the RTP.    However, the capacity charges and option payments associated with this

 2            prearranged purchase would be charged against current earnings. Thus, there is no

 3            incentive for GPC to prearrange purchases.


 4      Q     WHY IS IT REASONABLE TO REQUIRE GPC TO DISCLOSE ITS ENERGY

 5            PROCUREMENT PRACTICES?

 6      A     Although RTP is a regulated service, RTP customers are now exposed to competitive

 7            market price risks. As long as these customers cannot choose an alternative provider,

 8            they are entitled to know whether GPC's purchasing practices are reasonable and

 9            appropriate and that their interests are being adequately protected. Disclosure would

10            also give customers a better opportunity to access the risks and benefits of RTP. This

11            would also provide regulators with a more effective tool to ensure that the utility's power

12            procurement practices are reasonable and, further, that these practices result in the

13            lowest reasonable energy cost for all consumers.


14      Q     WHAT TYPES OF ENERGY PROCUREMENT PRACTICES SHOULD BE INCLUDED

15            IN A DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENT?

16     A      At a minimum, the Commission and the customers need a better understanding of the

17            various wholesale markets in which the utility is presently operating. This would include

18            both physical as well as financial markets. Specific wholesale markets (e.g., DA, HA,

19            options, swaps, etc.) and the different types of commercial transactions (e.g., 16-hour

20            strips, 8-hour strips, block sales at 100% load factor) should be identified.

21                   The Company should also reveal the evolution of specific transactions among the

22            various buyers and sellers. It would be especially insightful to know how many times a

23            particular transaction is purchased and sold, by whom and the extent to which the price

24            is adjusted before the final physical delivery occurs.

                                                                                    Jeffry Pollock
                                                                                          Page 30


               Finally, the Company should reveal the decision-making processes surrounding

2       the decision to participate in some markets but not others or to engage in certain types

3       of transactions.   To the extent that the Company's decisions are influenced by cost

4       recovery considerations, then this motivation should be clearly revealed.


5   Q   WOULD DISCLOSING ENERGY PROCUREMENT PRACTICES REQUIRE GPC TO

6       REVEAL CONFIDENTIAL TRADE SECRET INFORMATION?

7   A   No. There are adequate mechanisms already in place to ensure that confidential trade

8       secret information is not publicly disclosed. l n fact, many of the data responses in this

9       case and in other Commission proceedings are protected.

                               IV. The Commission Has Jurisdiction to
                             Grant the Relief Requested by the Petitioners


       Q'    WOULD GRANTING THE RELIEF REQUESTED IN THE PETITION REQUIRE THE

 2           COMMISSION TO REOPEN THE ACCOUNTING ORDER ADOPTED IN DOCKET

 3           NO. 9355-U?

 4     A     No. The requested relief will only affect two tariffs, RTP-DA and RTP-HA. Neither tariff

 5           was changed by the Accounting Order. 13

 6                      Second, the Petitioners are not asking the Commission to relitigate issues raised

 7           in GPC's last rate case. In fact, the serious problems with RTP had only just begun to

 8           surface in the spring of 1998, after the last rate case had been filed.         None of the

 9           evidence or arguments presented in this testimony was ever presented in the testimony

10           or the hearings in that case. RTP rate design was not specifically addressed.

11                      Finally, the Petitioners are not asking the Commission to change the terms of the

12           Accounting Order. The Accounting Order provides GPC with a reasonable opportunity

13          to earn a return on equity (ROE) of between 10% and 12.5%. Nothing in this Petition

14          would affect GPC's ability to earn within this range based on past experience under the

15          two Accounting Orders.


16     Q    IF THE COMMISSION WERE TO GRANT THE RELIEF REQUESTED IN THIS

17          PETITION, WILL IT AFFECT GPC'S EARNINGS?

18     A    Yes, it could. However, earnings are a function of both revenues and expenses. As the

19          Commission is well aware, revenues and expenses are not static. They will necessarily

20          change from the assumptions used to determine revenues and expenses or to assess

21          the appropriateness of a Accounting Order in GPC's last rate case.


            13
                 No other existing tariff was modified by the Accounting Order.

                                                            Grant the Relief Requested by the Petitioners

                                                                                            Jeffry Pollock
                                                                                                  Page 32


                     Revenues may increase or decrease depending on sales levels, economic

 2           conditions, weather and other factors.      Expenses may similarly increase or decrease

 3           based on the same factors and also on how well the Company manages its operations.
 4           A reduction in revenues to make the RTP tariffs fair, just and reasonable will not

 5           threaten GPC's ability to earn within the 10% to 12.5% range established in the

 6           Accounting Order.


 7   Q       HAVE GPC'S EARNINGS ALWAYS REMAINED WITHIN THIS RANGE?

 8   A       No. Since 1996, GPC's earned ROE has been 12.5% or higher. 14 In just the first year

 9           of the current Accounting Order, the Company reported earnings above a 12.5% ROE.

10           The amount of excess revenues was reported to be $105 million. As stated previously,

11           the excess margins collected from RTP customers account for about $63 million of this

12           excess revenue.


13   Q       DOES THE ACCOUNTING ORDER PROVIDE ANY GUARANTEE THAT GPC'S

14           EARNINGS WOULD FALL INTO THIS RANGE?

15   A       No. The Accounting Ortier most certainly does not guarantee that GPC will earn at least

16           at 12.5% ROE.       It does provide a reasonable opportunity for GPC to earn a 10% to

17           12.5% ROE.        There are also specific mechanisms in place to keep GPC's earnings

18          within this range. For example, if GPC earns more than 12.5% ROE in the year 2000,

19          then two-thirds of all of the excess revenues will be returned to customers. 15 Likewise, if

20           GPC's earnings drop below a 10% ROE, then GPC can petition the Commission to

21           increase rates.


            14
              1gnoring accelerated depreciation, GPC's earnings have consistently exceeded a 12.5% ROE.
            15
              1n the years 2000 and 2001, the Company gets to keep the first $50 million of excess revenue
     above a 12.5% ROE. Two-thirds of excess revenues above $50 million will be returned to customers.

     Q   WOULD CHANGING THE RTP TARIFFS AT THIS TIME BE CONSISTENT WITH THE

 2       ACCOUNTING ORDER?

 3   A   Yes.    The Accounting Order specifically states that the Commission retains its

 4       jurisdiction to ensure that the Company's rates are fair, just and reasonable. The Order

 5       also specifically provides for consideration of lambda averaging.            As I have

 6       demonstrated above, RTP is no longer fair, just and reasonable.        RTP prices have

 7       escalated dramatically and the Company has profited handsomely as a result.          The

 8       requested relief must be granted in full to restore fairness, justness and reasonableness

 9       to the RTP rates.

1O              Finally, to the extent that any future over-earnings are to be refunded to

11       customers, the Commission retains jurisdiction to allocate the over-earnings to all

12       customers, including RTP. RTP customers should receive a proportional share of any

13       excess revenues refunded by GPC.

15   A   Yes, it does.

                Direct Testimony of Jeffry Pollock Executive Summary 1 Real Time Pricing was an innovative cost based rate that was very beneficial for both 2 Georgia Power Company and its customers when it was introduced in 1992 It allowed the 3 customers a means to moderate standard industrial tariffs which are uncompetitive with 4 surrounding states so that the customer s total blended cost would remain competitive The rate 5 gave Georgia Power Company a powerful tool to compete for new industry with rates substantially 6 less than the regular standard tariff rates charged to its existing customers 7 As Georgia Power Company s capacity reserves decreased during the 90 s the RTP load 8 was served by increasingly expensive native generation and most significantly purchase power 9 This included spot purchases which are exceedingly expensive and will remain so until the 10 deregulated wholesale markets mature and sufficient merchant capacity is attracted to Georgia to 11 serve available customers While hot summers have been blamed for escalating RTP prices in 12 the past two years the price increases and volatility are more attributable to Georgia Power 13 Company s apparent unwillingness to protect its captive customers from the extreme high prices i Executive Summary BRUBAKER ASSOCIATES INC t w n       1       lr   r r                 1Tr       1T       TT Ili I T1 and volatility caused by tight capacity supplies and price deregulated wholesale markets Under 2 this scenario the flaws and inequities of the existing tariff structure have become pronounced with 3 the result that RTP prices have increased at an average of almost 7 a year since 1992 Because 4 of these changing circumstances RTP is no longer a cost based rate 5 The GTMA GIG Petition and this testimony identify the specific ways that the tariffs can be 6 modified to restore the cost basis and to more equitably balance the risks until a more permanent 7 cost based option of purchasing electricity can be allowed to industrial customers These areas of 8 adjustment are as follows 9 First remove the risk adder of 0 5 per kWh 0 45 for RTP HA As the 10 RTP tariffs are applied by GPC the Company has no risk All risk has been 11 shifted to the customer The margins from RTP sales are excessive and 12 unreasonable Removing the adder will restore the margins to a more 13 reasonable level that more clearly reflects the cost to provide the service 14 Second require GPC to properly administer the RTP tariffs or implement 15 lambda averaging The RTP tariffs do not allow purchased power costs to 16 be included in the hourly price contrary to actual practice This practice 17 should cease immediately Alternatively the price should be based on the 18 average cost of the native and purchased energy resources used to supply 19 RTP i e lambda averaging so that it reflects the actual cost of the power 20 GPC prices RTP at the cost of the last and most expensive resource 21 employed This practice is tantamount to selling a lot full of Ford 22 automobiles at a Mercedes price just because one Mercedes happens to be 23 parked on the same lot 24 Third modify the fuel accounting to reflect the actual real time cost of the 25 generated or purchased energy used to set the hourly prices This 26 practice will avoid an artificial underrecovery of fuel under the Georgia 27 Power interpretation Any underrecovery is separately and additionally 28 recovered from all customers 29 Fourth require accountability by Georgia Power Company to its 30 customers for its purchasing practices The design of the RTP rate offers 31 no incentive to GPC to purchase energy for the least dollar cost and the 32 customers presently have no right to seek lower cost suppliers of 33 electricity 34 These changes can be made without reopening or violating the terms of the Accounting 35 Order approved in GPC s last rate case Docket No 9355 U The Accounting Order cannot and 36 should not be used as an excuse to deny the Petition to make only a temporary fix in the rate or ii Executive Summary BRUBAKER ASSOCIATES INC T Ill I flll T f lltTT                    T T F II I I 111 wait 5 1 using RTP is that the total blended cost of electricity can be more competitive than the 2 standard firm rates 3 Q HOW HAS THE RTP RATE HISTORICALLY HELPED TO MAKE GPC S RATES 4 MORE COMPETITIVE 5 A RTP has historically been used in conjunction with a standard tariff to allow customers to 6 reduce their average cost of electricity 7 RTP was designed to be a cost based rate option designed to                                        II. Why the Petition Was Filed


         1   Q   WHY DID GTMA AND GIG FILE THE PETITION FOR RULE NISI?

         2   A   The GTMA/GIG Petition was filed to address serious problems with GPC's RTP tariffs.

         3       These serious problems include:

         4       1.     Concerns about the overall competitiveness of GPC's rates in light of recent
         5              drastic increases in average RTP prices;

         6       2.     The RTP tariffs are not being properly applied because purchased power costs
         7              are included in the hourly running cost of incremental generation; and

         8       3.     Dramatic changes in circumstances since the inception of RTP have resulted in
         9              prices that are no longer fair, just and reasonable and which are providing
        10              excessive revenues to GPC. As explained below, certain of the design
        11              parameters of the RTP tariffs need to be updated in order to bring the rate more
        12              in line with cost and to mitigate the excess revenues being enjoyed by GPC at its
        13              customers' expense.


        14   Q   WHY IS IT NECESSARY FOR GPC TO OFFER RTP?

        15   A   GPC's standard rates are more expensive than the corresponding standard rates of

        16       other utilities in the southeastern United States. This is shown in Exhibit _ _ (JP-1).

        17       As can be seen from this Exhibit, all three comparisons demonstrate that GPC's

        18       standard industrial tariff is priced well-above the average rate for similar service offered

        19       by investor-owned utilities (IOU) in the Southeast.        For example, page 1 shows that,

        20       based on industrial rates in effect on July 1, 1998, GPC ranked 15th out of 40

        21       southeastern IOUs. (A ranking of 1 is the most expensive, and a ranking of 40 is the

        22       least expensive.) By July 1, 1999 (page 2), GPC ranked 14th most expensive. This

        23       means that 25 and 26 other Southeastern IOUs priced their standard industrial service

        24       below GPC, respectively in 1998 and 1999.


                                                                              II. Why the Petition Was Filed

                                              BRUBAKER & AsSOCIATES, !NC.


                                    T - 1r-T T - .. --

                                                                                         STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment A


                                                                                       Jeffry Pollock'   48
                                                                                              Page4


 1               The rankings shown on pages 1 and 2 were developed from various Edison

 2       Electric Institute (EEi) publications for an industrial customer having a 68% monthly load

 3       factor, which is consistent with EEi's assumptions.


 4   Q   DO GPC'S STANDARD RATES COMPARE MORE FAVORABLY FOR HIGHER LOAD

 5       FACTOR CUSTOMERS?

 6   A   No. Exhibit _ _ (JP-1), page 3, shows the results of a BAI survey of rates in effect on

 7       January 1, 2000 for 90% load factor customers. Further, unlike the prior EEi surveys,

 8       SAi's Southeastern Survey includes a major competitor to GPC, the Tennessee Valley

 9       Authority (TVA).

10               The BAI survey confirms that GPC's standard industrial tariffs are priced above

11       the average.       Specifically, GPC is the 10th most expensive out of 33 utilities in the

12       survey. This means that 23 other utilities, including TVA, charged less for industrial high

13       load factor service than GPC.


14   Q   HOW IS RTP USED IN CONJUNCTION WITH GPC'S STANDARD TARIFFS?

15   A   The standard tariffs apply to a customer's existing load prior to commencing RTP

16       service. This existing load is referred to as a customer baseline load (or CBL). RTP

17       applies to a customer's actual hourly loads when those loads differ from the CBL.

18               For example, if a customer's hourly load is above the CBL, the customer is

19       charged the hourly real time price.      Similarly, if a customer's hourly load is below the

20       CBL, the customer is paid the hourly real time price. If a customer continues to operate

21       at the CBL, then the customer would continue to pay the same total cost as under the

22       standard tariff.

23               Thus, customers that operate above the CBL during low-cost hours and/or below

"4       the CBL in high-cost hours will reduce their average cost of electricity. The net result of


                                                                      II. Why the Petition Was Filed
                                        BRUBAKER & AsSOCIATES, INC.

                                                                                                    STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment A


                                                                                                  Jeffry Pofi'ock   48
                                                                                                         Pages


             using RTP is that the total blended cost of electricity can be more competitive than the

 2           standard firm rates.


 3   Q       HOW HAS THE RTP RATE HISTORICALLY HELPED TO MAKE GPC'S RATES

 4           MORE COMPETITIVE?

 5   A       RTP has historically been used in conjunction with a standard tariff to allow customers to

 6           reduce their average cost of electricity.

 7                      RTP was designed to be a cost-based rate option designed to reflect GPC's

 8           incremental cost of generation and transmission. The standard tariffs, by contrast, are

 9           designed to fully recover GPC's embedded cost, which include generation, transmission,

10           distribution and other overhead costs. Because the incremental cost of generation and

11           transmission is below GPC's overall embedded cost of service, RTP service costs less

12           than taking service under GPC's standard tariffs. As explained later, RTP is no longer a

13           cost-based rate and it is no longer providing a competitive advantage for GPC

14           customers.


15   Q       DOES GPC OFFER DIFFERENT TYPES OF REAL TIME PRICING SERVICE?

16   A       Yes.      GPC offers two RTP options:          Day-Ahead (DA) and Hour-Ahead (HA).             The

17           RTP-DA and RTP-HA tariffs are similar in structure.               Both require the customer to

18          establish a CBL, and the hourly prices include the running cost of incremental

19          generation, losses and a recovery factor or adder. 1 As discussed later, the adder is a flat

20          charge per kilowatthour (kWh) and it provides a contribution to fixed costs (i.e., profit).

21           Under certain circumstances, the hourly prices will include an outage factor and a charge


             1
                 Losses are added to the incremental generation cost because this cost is initially quoted at the
     power plant, and some energy is consumed to deliver electricity from the generator to a customer.


                                                                             II. Why the Petition Was Filed

                                               BRUBAKER & AsSOCIATES, INC.

                                                                                         STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment A


                                                                                       Jeffry PollQ~k.        O
                                                                                               Page6      5

         for incremental transmission. However, the running cost of incremental generation, or

 2       system lambda, is by far the most significant component of the hourly real time prices.


 3   Q   WHAT ARE THE KEY DIFFERENCES BETWEEN RTP-DA AND RTP-HA?

 4   A   There are two key differences. First, for RTP-DA customers, GPC determines by 4:00

 5       p.m. the 24 hourly prices applicable on the next day. This is in contrast to HA service

 6       where the price for each hour is not determined until one-hour before service

 7       commences.

 8              Second, the two RTP options have different adders. The DA adder is 0.5¢ per

 9       kWh, while the corresponding HA adder is 0.45¢ per kWh.


10   Q   HOW MUCH LOAD IS PRICED ON RTP VS. THE STANDARD TARIFFS?

11   A   RTP sales account for about 34% of the total energy sold to RTP customers.              The

12       remaining 66% is priced under a standard tariff.


13   Q   DO THE LOWER PRICES OFFERED BY RTP COME FREELY WITH NO RISK?

14   A   No.   Unlike any other retail customer served by GPC, RTP customers experience

15       immediate price level changes as a result of projected changes in the hourly running

16       cost of generation and purchased power.

17              For example, if GPC projects a need to purchase power on the wholesale spot

18       market at a cost of $6 per kWh, the same $6 per kWh cost, plus additional markups, will

19       be immediately reflected in the hourly RTP. If GPC does not effectively control these

20       costs, then it jeopardizes the competitiveness of the RTP program. This, in turn, further

21       jeopardizes the competitiveness of the customers that have come to rely upon RTP as a

22       way to keep jobs in Georgia.

     Q   IS PRICE VOLATILITY THE MAJOR ISSUE?

 3       Average RTP prices have increased drastically during the summers of 1998 and 1999.

       Q    WHY DO YOU CONTEND THAT GPC HAS IMPROPERLY INCLUDED PURCHASED

 2          POWER COSTS IN DETERMINING THE HOURLY PRICES?
 3     A    The approved RTP tariffs state that "the hourly prices are based on projections of the

4           hourly running cost of incremental generation." (emphasis added) However, generation

 5          is not functionally equivalent to purchased power.            Generation means electricity

 6          produced by a utility from power plants that the utility owns.         Purchased power, by

 7          contrast, refers to electricity purchased by a utility from resources that are owned by a

 8          third party - either a utility, a marketer or a non-utility generator (NUG).


 9     Q    IS THERE ALSO A DISTINCTION BETWEEN GENERATION AND PURCHASED

10          POWER IN GENERALLY ACCEPTED ACCOUNTING PRACTICE?

11     A    Yes.   The FERC System of Accounts also distinguishes between generation-related

12          expenses and purchased power. Specifically, generation-related expenses are booked

13          to Accounts 500 through 554.        Purchased power costs, by contrast, are booked to

14          Account 555.


15     Q    DOES THIS COMMISSION RECOGNIZE THAT GENERATION AND PURCHASED

16          POWER ARE NOT FUNCTIONALLY EQUIVALENT?

17     A    Yes.   GPC's FCR tariff distinguishes between the cost of energy generated and the

18          energy cost of purchased power. If generation and purchased power were the same,

19          then there would have been no need for a separate reference to purchased power.

 1      Q        WAS THERE ANY INDICATION THAT GPC HAD INTENDED TO INCLUDE

 2               PURCHASED POWER IN THE HOURLY REAL TIME PRICES WHEN RTP WAS

 3               FIRST IMPLEMENTED?

 4      A        No.   The testimony sponsored by GPC witnesses in 1992 made no mention that

 5               purchased power cost would be included in determining the hourly running cost of

 6               incremental generation, or system lambda. Specifically, the term system lambda was

 7               used synonymously with incremental plant operating costs. 2 This same testimony goes

 8               on to state that "the magnitude of this cost [incremental plant operating cost] will vary

 9               with the hourly mix of generation resources that are then in use for meeting Georgia

10               Power Company's territorial load. "3


11      Q        WHY ELSE IS INCLUDING PURCHASED POWER IN DETERMINING THE HOURLY

12               RTPs NOT APPROPRIATE?

13      A        Wholesale power markets have changed dramatically since the inception of RTP in

14               Georgia.    The Energy Policy Act of 1992 gave the Federal Energy Regulatory

15               Commission (FERC) authority to require all utilities under its jurisdiction to provide open

16               nondiscriminatory access to the transmission system. The FERC subsequently issued

17               Order No. 888 in April 1996. The effect of Order No. 888 has been a dramatic increase

18               in the use of transmission services by third parties. This, in turn, has reduced the vertical

19               market power of transmission-owning utilities. The FERC has granted authority to allow

20               utilities and other wholesale market participants to buy and sell electricity at market-

21               based prices. This, coupled with the movement to customer choice by 24 states, has

22               resulted in a wholesale market that today is, for all intents and purposes, price

23               deregulated.

        Companl., Docket No. 4147-U, May 11, 1992, page 10. (emphasis added)

                    By including spot wholesale purchases in the hourly RTPs, GPC's captive

 2       customers are now being exposed to more price risk than ever before.                      As stated

 3       previously, a projected market-based purchased power transaction, as high as $6 per

 4       kWh in· 1999, will immediately be reflected in the hourly price. No other retail customer

 5       will immediately see this $6 per kWh price.4 If the power is actually purchased, then the

 6       cost will be charged to the fuel account and passed through to all customers.                   This

 7       automatic pass-through of actual fuel and purchased energy costs demonstrates that

 8       GPC bears absolutely no risk to provide RTP service.

 9                  Although RTP is a regulated service, the hourly prices are increasingly being

10       influenced by the deregulated wholesale market. Fairness demands that if a regulated

11       tariff allows the pass-through of deregulated prices, then the captive customers should

12       have more options than simply reducing load to offset the higher prices.                   The most

13       effective option is to allow the customer to choose an alternative supplier. However, until

14       customer choice is authorized in Georgia, the Commission must continue to function as

15       a "surrogate for competition" to ensure that regulated prices are fair, just and reasonable.

                                  Ill. The Requested Relief


 1   Q   WHAT RELIEF ARE GTMA AND GIG SEEKING IN THE PETITION?

 2   A   The Petition asks the Commission to modify the RTP tariffs in light of the dramatically

 3       changing circumstances and the much greater price risk placed on RTP customers. The

 4       suggested modifications would restore the competitiveness to the industrial rates,

 5       provide a more equitable balancing of the risks between GPC and its captive RTP

 6       customers and would benefit all customers by reducing the FCR.


 7   Q   HOW SHOULD THE RTP TARIFFS BE MODIFIED?

 8   A   The specific modifications should include:

 9       1.     Eliminating the adders entirely or, at a minimum, reducing the adders by at least
10              50%.
11       2.     Lambda averaging; and

12       3.     Revising the fuel cost accounting.


13   Q   IF THE COMMISSION WERE TO ORDER THE REMOVAL OF PURCHASED POWER

14       FROM THE SYSTEM LAMBDA CALCULATION, WOULD LAMBDA AVERAGING BE

15       NECESSARY?

16   A   No. However, the adders should also be eliminated or reduced to make RTP fair, just

17       and reasonable.


18   Q   WHAT OTHER RELIEF DOES THE PETITION REQUEST?

19   A   The Petition also requests the Commission to establish standards to require GPC to

20       disclose its energy procurement practices.

 1   Adder
2    Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE ADDER?

 3   A   The adder is a fixed amount that is charged for every RTP kWh purchased or sold. At

 4       present, the adder is 0.5¢ under RTP-DA and 0.45¢ under RTP-HA.


 5   Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THE ADDER?

 6   A   The adder was originally designed to serve two purposes.             First, it provided a

 7       contribution to fixed costs (i.e., profit).     Second, it compensated GPC for the risks

 8       associated with RTP. This is perhaps why GPC originally described the adder as a "risk

 9       recovery factor." 9


10   Q   WHY IS IT NECESSARY FOR RTP CUSTOMERS TO PROVIDE A CONTRIBUTION

11       TO FIXED COSTS?

12   A   Every rate should provide some contribution of fixed costs or profit, and RTP is no

13       exception.       If RTP sales provide some revenue to defray GPC's fixed costs, all other

14           non-RTP customers will benefit. This is because the margins generated from RTP sales

15       will lower the revenue requirement recoverable from, and the rates chargeable to, non-

16           RTP customers.


17   Q   WHAT RISKS WERE INITIALLY ATTRIBUTABLE TO RTP?

18   A   While other utilities were beginning to implement small scale experimental programs,

19           GPC was seeking Commission approval for a full-scale RTP program. At that time, RTP

20       was still a novel pricing mechanism.        GPC did not have much experience projecting

21           hourly real time prices on a day-ahead basis. There was a risk that the quoted day-

22           ahead prices would understate actual energy costs.

         9
             ld., Footnote 1.

                                         BRUBAKER & AsSOCIATES, !NC.

                                                                                                   STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment A


                                                                                               Jeffry Pollo'ck    61
                                                                                                      Page 17


                      Finally, GPC did not know how customers would respond to RTP. To the extent

 2            that customers' response was more than the Company had anticipated, this could

 3            produce revenue erosion. The risk recovery factor was designed to offset this erosion

 4            and the other risks associated with RTP.


 5    Q       IS AN ADDER STILL APPROPRIATE IN TODAY'S CIRCUMSTANCES?

 6    A       No. When RTP was first implemented, marginal energy costs and embedded energy

 7            costs were similar. Thus, the 0.5¢ adder was necessary to ensure that every kWh sold

 8            under RTP would provide some contribution toward fixed cost recovery or profit. Today,

 9            however, marginal energy costs are much higher than embedded energy costs. This

10            means that every kWh sold under RTP already provides some profit without the need for

11            an additional 0.5¢ (or 0.45¢) adder.


12    Q       DO OTHER UTILITIES IMPOSE A FIXED ADDER ON ALL RTP KWh SALES?

13    A       Yes.   Some southeast utilities, like Duke Power Company and Virginia Electric and

14            Power Company, do charge a flat adder for all RTP kWh sold. Duke Power Company's

15            adder is 0.5¢, the same as GPC's RTP-DA tariff. Virginia Electric and Power Company

16            charges a 0.6¢ adder on RTP sales. However, both utilities have lower standard rates

17            than GPC. 1  ° Further, Duke Power's average real time prices were lower and less
18            volatile than GPC's during the summers of 1998 and 1999.

.1     Q    IS A FLAT CENTS PER KWh ADDER A UNIVERSAL PRACTICE?

 2     A    No. Several southeast utilities charge a variable adder. These utilities include Carolina

 3          Power & Light Company, Central Power and Light Company, FPL and Southwestern

 4          Electric Power Company. The variable adder is stated as a percentage of the difference

 5          between the average cost per kWh under the standard tariff and the corresponding

 6          hourly marginal energy cost.

 7                 For example, assume that a standard tariff has an average cost of 4¢ per kWh

 8          and the utility is allowed to retain 20% of the difference between the standard tariff and

 9          marginal energy cost. If the marginal energy cost were 2¢, then the adder would be

10          0.4¢ per kWh [20% x (4¢ - 2¢)]. On the other hand, if marginal energy costs were above

11          4¢, then no adder would be charged. The latter circumstance is most likely to occur

12          during extreme hot weather conditions, when generation supplies are tight, and/or the

13          utility is having to purchase spot-market energy to satisfy customer demand.


14     Q    IS THE ADDER NEEDED TO PROVIDE A REASONABLE CONTRIBUTION TO GPC'S

15          FIXED COSTS, OR PROFIT?

16     A    No.   RTP sales are generating sufficient margins without the adder to provide a

17          reasonable contribution to GPC's fixed costs, or profit.

 1   a   SHOULD THE. ADDER BE RETAINED TO COMPENSATE FOR THE RISKS

 2       ASSOCIATED WITH RTP?
 3   A   No.   GPC has had seven years of experience with RTP.                RTP is no longer a novel

 4       pricing mechanism. Today, many utilities nationwide, including many in the Southeast,

 5       also offer RTP.

 6              Further, GPC's fears about revenue erosion have been unfounded. RTP sales

 7       above the CBL are more than 14 times higher than RTP sales below the CBL. This is

 8       shown in Exhibit _ _ (JP-7).

 9              There is no risk of underrecovery as a result of underforecasting day-ahead

1O       energy prices.    This is because all eligible fuel and purchased energy costs are

11       recovered to the FCR. Finally, GPCs allowed return on equity already includes a risk

12       premium. No further risk adjustment is necessary.


13   Q   PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR RECOMMENDATION REGARDING THE ADDER?

14   A   The adder should be eliminated because it is no longer needed to provide a reasonable

15       contribution to fixed costs and because it is no longer necessary to compensate GPC for

16       the risks associated with the RTP program. RTP is now more risky for GPC's captive

17       customers. Eliminating the adder would be the most direct way to compensate these

18       customers for the added risk.


19   Q   WHAT WOULD BE THE IMPACT OF ELIMINATING THE ADDER?

20   A   The adders in the RTP-DA and RTP-HA rates generate about $46.2 million a year in

21       revenue. A 50% reduction would lower GPC's annual revenue by only $23.1 million, or

22       about 0.5%.

 1   Lambda Averaging

 2   Q   WHAT IS SYSTEM LAMBDA?.

 3   A   System lambda is the term used to describe the hourly running cost of incremental

 4       generation.    It consists primarily of incremental fuel cost and a small amount of

 5       incremental variable operation and maintenance expense (VOM).


 6   Q   HOW DOES GPC DEFINE SYSTEM LAMBDA IN THE CONTEXT OF THE RTP

 7       TARIFFS?

 8   A   System lambda is not defined in the RTP tariffs. GPC chooses to define system lambda

 9       as the cost of the next kWh generated or purchased to serve territorial load.      This

10       definition is illustrated in Exhibit __ (JP-8).

11              The illustration is a hypothetical example of a series of resources (either

12       generation or purchased power) that have been dispatched to serve 1,000 megawatts

13       (MW) of RTP load in a given hour. In this hypothetical, the resources are assumed to be

14       equal in size and range in cost from 3¢ to 7¢ per kWh.

15               Based on this hypothetical example, the system lambda employed by GPC in the

16       RTP tariffs would be 7¢ per kWh. Consequently, all RTP sales in this hour would be

17       priced to reflect the 7¢ system lambda, even though the vast majority of the kWh serving

18       RTP load would cost much less.


19   Q   WHAT IS MEANT BY THE TERM LAMBDA AVERAGING?

20   A   Lambda averaging means calculating the weighted average cost of resources operating

21       on the margin to serve a particular block of load. Using the illustration in Exhibit __

22       (JP-8), lambda averaging applied to 1,000 MW of RTP load would result in a charge of

23       only 5¢ per kWh.
