11
12   A.      It could for a particular year if that year is extremely hot like 1998 and 1999. But, if
13           future years return to normal weather, RTP will not rise dramatically and will be below
14           those levels observed in 1998 and 1999. In fact, our expected RTP-DA price for 2000 is
15           (Redacted) cents/kWh (2000 RTP-DA expected price), which is (Redacted)
16           (percentage reduction in RTP-DA price for 2000) below the 1999 actual. (Please see
17           Exhibit_(HK0-13)). And, with some of the new rate alternatives included in this
18           filing, we are willing to assure our RTP customers who take these options that this will be
19           the most they will have to pay for any RTP load that they want to place on the alternative.
20
21   Q.      DO YOU EXPECT THE RTP PRICES TO CONTINUE TO REMAIN HIGH OR
22           MODERATE?
23
24   A.      Since the high RTP prices are related to: extreme weather conditions; unit outages;
25           regional reserves; and the spot market price of purchase, we expect that RTP prices will
26           moderate over time. The reason for this is simple. Since the current high spot market
27           prices are a result of a tight supply market, we believe that the industry and independent
28           developers are responding to this tight market by adding significant amounts of new
29           capacity in the Southeast and around the nation. As these new resources become
30           available to the market, the prices paid in the spot market should moderate and be lower
31           cost in real terms. Thus, the RTP price signals should reflect this change as well.
32
33   Q.      MR. POLLOCK STATED THAT 1999 WAS NOT THAT HOT A YEAR, AND
34           YOU'RE SAYING THAT HOT WEATHER DID CAUSE THE HIGH 1999
35           PRICES. HOW DO YOU EXPLAIN THIS?
36
37   A.      While it is true that the summer of 1998 was hotter on average than the summer of 1999,
38           the summer of 1998 heat was spread throughout the summer months and not concentrated
39           in any one period. On the other hand, the period between July and the end of August
40           1999 had more extreme weather than any comparable period in 1998. For instance,
41           August 1999 had 21.5% more cooling degree days than a normal August. This 21.5%
42           difference in cooling degree days was higher than the difference between actual and
43           normal weather for any summer month in 1998. This concentration of extreme
44           temperatures in late July and early August drove the peak load to record levels day after
45           day, thus contributing to record-level wholesale spot market prices and extreme RTP
46           prices.


     Note: Bold faced type in answers indicates trade secret material. Please refer to the assigned name when      24
            discussing.


                                                                   ·-·---·- I ,II                               I 11

                                                                                                                STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment B


2            An indication of the difference in the concentration of heat during 1999 can be seen in the
3            energy weighted maximum temperatures. Georgia Power Company uses seven weather
4            stations located across the state. These hourly temperatures of weather stations are
5            weighted based on energy consumption for the area surrounding each station. This
6            weighting provides an hourly temperature that is representative of Georgia Power's entire
7            service area. During 1998, the maximum hourly weighted temperature for the year was
 8           only 96.2 degrees. However, in 1999 the maximum hourly weighted temperature for the
 9           year was 98.8 degrees, a difference of almost 2.6 degrees. Moreover, 1999 had a period
10           of about a week with such extreme temperatures. Even though over the course of the
11           entire year, 1999 was slightly cooler than 1998, the extended high temperatures in 1999
12           had a very significant impact on peak demand and RTP prices.
13
14           We are a summer peaking utility. Each individual hour is critical and its load must be
15           served. As a utility becomes constrained, its hourly marginal cost accelerates at a non-
16           linear, exponential rate. In other words, a one degree temperature change in a summer
17           afternoon day averaging 95QF can have an extraordinary influence on load, while a one
18           degree temperature change when the temperature is averaging 85 2F can have a very mild
19           influence. (One-degree change when temperatures are in the 90's can add 750mW's of
20           load to the SES). One cannot merely look at overall heating degree and cooling degree
21           days for the year to ascertain if weather has influenced load and prices. If during one
22           hour the actual temperature were 84QF instead of the expected 85QF, and in another hour
23           the actual temperature were 96QF instead of the expected 95 2F, Mr. Pollock's
24           methodology would ask you to believe that you had normal weather over these two
25           hours, and therefore, loads and prices should be normal.
26
27   Q.      WERE THERE SPECIFIC CRITICAL TIME PERIODS DURING 1999 WHEN
28           TEMPERATURES AND LOADS WERE EXTRAORDINARILY HIGH?
29
30   A.      For the first 6% months of 1999, the weather was somewhat normal, and prices were near
31           expectations. Then on July 23 a heat wave came across the U.S. and lasted through
32           August. The cooling degree days (CDDs) from 7/23/99-8/31199 in the territory that we
33           serve were the hottest ever recorded, amounting to over 20% above the average of the
34           past 20 years! Loads skyrocketed with the SES setting numerous all-time peaks along
35           with many other utilities (some of these other utilities even experienced blackouts). As a
36           result, wholesale prices and RTP prices skyrocketed during this period. The result was
37           average RTP prices for July and August at extremely high levels (note the one hot week
38           in July caused prices that week that more than offset the relatively mild RTP prices for
39           the first three weeks of July). The average RTP price for 1999 was greatly influenced by
40           these two months. The 1998 peak was exceeded for a total of 64 hours during late July
41           and early August. The bottom line is, we don't expect extraordinary weather patterns like
42           this to continue. We have RTP price expectations reflecting this belief, and we're willing
43           to offer RTP Alternatives that will assure the customers of these prices.

         Q.          WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THE RTP ALTERNATIVES?
 2
  3      A.          The RTP Alternatives are excellent pricing solutions for RTP customers who have a need
  4                  for additional control over their exposure to RTP prices. The purpose of the RTP
  5                  Alternatives is to allow RTP customers to manage. reduce or remove price risk associated
  6                  with RTP. While many RTP customers will prefer to stay on the RTP tariff, others will
  7                  have the opportunity to move to an alternative that will provide more stability and
  8                  certainty than RTP alone. They are not to replace RTP or to suggest that RTP is not a
  9                  good tariff that is doing what it was designed to do.
10
11       Q.          WHY HAS GPC FILED AND OFFERED THE RTP ALTERNATIVES?
12
13       A.          First of all, many customers want more pricing options and more control over their
14                   electricity costs. GPC always desires to meet the needs of our customers with innovative
 15                  pricing products. For example, GPC has supported the offering of Price Protection
 16                  Products to RTP customers for several years. The portfolio of new RTP Alternatives will
 17                  successfully meet the needs of RTP customers to mitigate RTP price risk. The
 18                  Alternatives provide fair, reasonable and competitive rate options. They are excellent
 19                  pricing solutions for RTP customers.
20
21                   Second, customers have requested the development and offering of these specific rate
22                   alternatives. The W.A.N.T. Project (What Are The Needs Today; see Exhibit_(HK0-
23                   14)) was a year-long Georgia Power initiative in 1999 aimed at developing innovative
 24                  pricing products to meet the needs in our marketplace. In this extensive market research
 25                  project, we surveyed and interviewed many RTP customers to understand their needs.
 26                  We designed the Alternatives around their needs and tested the Alternatives with those
 27                  customers. Customer feedback on this package of Alternatives has been clearly positive
 28                  and favorable because of the Alternatives' ability to alleviate risk at fair and reasonable
 29                  prices.
 30
 31       Q.          BRIEFLY DESCRIBE THE RTP ALTERNATIVES.
 32
 33       A.          A general analogy to illustrate the value of the RTP Alternatives would be home
 34                   mortgage rate options. A prospective homeowner's alternatives for paying the mortgage
 35                   company for the loan service include a range of choices, from purely adjustable rates to
 36                   30-year fixed rates. The adjustable mortgage rates obviously represent RTP in this
 37                   analogy, and the range of other alternatives, which could be part-adjustable/part-fixed
 38                   options or completely fixed options, represent the new RTP Alternatives. With the
 39                   adjustable mortgage rates and RTP, you take on more risk to get access to the lower cost.
 40                   With the fixed mortgage rates and the RTP Alternatives, you agree to pay a little more to
 41                   lock in an attractive rate and protect yourself against possible increases during some
 42                   periods of time.
 43
 44                   GPC proposes the following four RTP Alternatives. A tabular summary is provided as
 45                   well as a brief written description on each of the Alternatives. In addition, a "scorecard"
 46                   on specific attributes is shown on Exhibit_(HK0-15).

3            1)       RTP with Adjustable CBL
4
5            RTP with Adjustable CBL allows an RTP customer to manage RTP price risk. The
6            customer may adjust the Customer Baseline Load (CBL) once a year to manage the level
7            of exposure to RTP prices. The customer may select to raise the CBL for a twelve-month
 8           period in order to lock in expected RTP prices for some or all of the incremental load. Or
9            the customer may select to lower the CBL for a twelve-month period in order to apply
10           RTP prices to more load. The monthly Standard Bills will be recalculated to reflect the
11           adjustment to the CBL. See Exhibit_(HK0-16-1) and (HK0-16-2) for illustrations.
12           Refer to Exhibits_(HK0-16-3) and (HK0-16-4) for copies of the tariffs.
13
14           2)       RTP with Price Protection Products
15
16           RTP with Price Protection Products (PPP) allows a RTP customer to manage RTP price
17           risk. PPPs are separate financial hedge contracts (Caps, CIDs, Collars and Index Prices)
18           that may be used to achieve price stability during specific time periods. GPC has offered
19           PPPs on a limited, pilot basis in the past and seeks to improve and expand the program to
20           more customers with more products. See Exhibits_(HK0-17-1) and (HK0-17-2) and
21           (HK0-17-3) for an example. Refer to Exhibit_(HK0-17-4) for a copy of the tariff.
22
23           3)       Variable Incremental Pricing
24
25           Variable Incremental Pricing (VIP) allows a RTP customer to reduce RTP price risk.
26           VIP provides TOU pricing in most hours for the incremental load, that is, load in excess
27           of the CBL. The incremental load is interruptible for both economic and reliability
28           considerations. During the economic and reliability periods the customer may choose to
29           "buy through" by paying RTP-HA (Hour Ahead) prices and RTP-HA plus $3.50/kWh,
30           respectively. VIP should be thought of as a non-RTP rate alternative. In fact, it is similar
31           to PL plus the SE rider, but with a lot of improvements. See Exhibit_(HK0-18-1) for
32           an illustration. Refer to Exhibit_(HK0-18-2) for a copy of the tariff.
33
34           4)       Fixed Incremental Pricing
35
36           Fixed Incremental Pricing (FIP) allows an RTP customer to remove RTP price risk. FIP
37           provides simple, fixed, firm Time-Of-Use (TOU) pricing for those customers who prefer
38           a stable price. To simplify the pricing and billing under this tariff, all of the customer's
39           usage is actually priced at the FIP TOU energy charges, and a fixed charge is developed

     Note: Bold faced type in answers indicates trade secret material. Please refer to the assigned name when   27
            discussing.

                                                                                                                STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment B


             to cover the fixed costs of serving the customer. This economic TOU tariff should also
 2           be thought of as a non-RTP rate alternative. It is a simple, economically priced TOU
 3           rate.   Refer to Exhibit_(HK0-19) for a copy of the tariff.            Refer also to
 4           Exhibit_(HK0-20) for an updated version of the Large Business Reduction Rider
 5           (LBR-2) which now includes FIP. See Exhibit_(HK0-21) for an example.
 6

 8           Exhibit_(HK0-23) which illustrates cost versus price risk for the RTP Alternatives.

24   SPECIFIC ERRORS                       AND         MISSTATEMENT                    IN      PETITIONER'S
2s   TESTIMONY
26
27   Q.      DID MR. POLLOCK CORRECTLY CALCULATE THE REVENUE VARIANCE
28           ASSOCIATED WITH HIGH REAL TIME PRICES IN 1999?
29
30   A.      No, the $63 million figure calculated by Mr. Pollock is incorrect. Actual RTP revenues
31           during 1999 were $48,976,678 above the forecasted revenues. Since total 1999 Georgia
32           Power revenues were $131. 7 million over the forecasted revenues, the RTP revenue
33           variance was about 37% of the total, instead of 60% quoted by Mr. Pollock. For
34           comparison, 14.5% of the revenue variance was supplied by residential customers and
35           50% of the revenues variance was supplied by commercial customers.
36
37   Q.      DO YOU AGREE WITH MR. POLLOCK WHERE HE STATES THAT RTP IS
38           NO LONGER A COST-BASED RATE BECAUSE OF GPC'S " ... APPARENT
39           UNWILLINGNESS TO PROTECT ITS CAPTIVE CUSTOMERS FROM THE
40           EXTREME HIGH PRICES AND VOLATILITY CAUSED BY TIGHT
41           CAPACITY SUPPLIES ... "?
42
43   A.      No. This is not a true statement, but demonstrates a misunderstanding of the difference
44           between marginal costs and average costs. Rates based on real time system lambda
45           (system incremental cost) are inherently both marginal cost based and volatile. System
46           incremental cost, as calculated in real time, is highly sensitive to the available system

     Note: Bold faced type in answers indicates trade secret material. Please refer to the assigned name when   29
            discussing.

                                                                                                                STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment B


             generation mix (which is subject to resource outage variations), load variations (which
2            are in turn highly sensitive to weather variations) and various congestion factors, all of
3            which can be and are monetized for use in the calculation of RTP prices. This is
4            distinctly different from average cost methodology where volatility is averaged out over
5            time.
 6
 7           Mr. Pollock states that "... the RTP tariffs do not allow purchased power costs to be
 8           included in the hourly price ... " This is not true. The original RTP tariff was developed
 9           based on the resource stack concept utilized by Southern Company for economic dispatch
10           and unit commitment. Power purchases were considered a part of the resource stack and
11           included in the calculation of system incremental costs at the time RTP was developed as
12           they are today. They were not nearly as common at that time, but they were part of the
13           stack. The Resource Stack concept was used at Southern Company and throughout the
14           electric utility industry considerably prior to the development of the RTP tariff. In this
15           concept, all dispatchable resources, including both generation and purchases as well as
16           (potentially) economically driven interruptible customers, are included in a resource stack
17           that is ordered on an economic basis. Resources are drawn from the stack to serve
18           system needs as required and the economic point in the stack from which the resource is
19           drawn effectively sets system incremental cost or lambda. All dispatchable resources are
20           included in the stack unless specifically excluded for contractual or technical reasons.
21
22   Q.      CAN YOU COMMENT ON MR. POLLOCK'S COMPLAINTS ON THE
23           INCREASE IN RTP PRICES?
24
25   A.      There is no doubt that 1998 and 1999 RTP prices have been higher. One must be
26           cautious however in presuming that the most recent two years are absolute indicators of
27           the future. Please see Exhibit_(HK0-24) for the RTP price increase over the first 5
28           years. As we have stated earlier, the last two years have had extraordinary weather
29           conditions when compared to the past 20 years. In addition, the cycle of this capital
30           intensive industry in terms of capacity is very relevant. Exhibit_(HK0-25) shows an
31           expected RTP price growth rate from inception to expected year 2000.
32
33   Q.      IS MR. POLLOCK'S ANALOGY OF "SELLING A LOT FULL OF FORD
34           AUTOMOBILES AT A MERCEDES PRICE JUST BECAUSE ONE MERCEDES
35           HAPPENS TO BE PARKED ON THE SAME LOT" A FAIR ANALOGY?
36
37   A.      No, absolutely not. Whether a kWh is generated by a base load unit, a combustion
38           turbine, or a purchase, that kWh is identical in make-up. To use his construct you have a
39           lot full of identical kWhs. The fact is that the last kWhs that you added to the lot are
40           expensive, in fact the most expensive on the lot and indicative of what you will have to
41           pay to add additional kWhs to your lot and possibly the future cost to replace any kWhs
42           currently on your lot. So the products are sold on your lot at this recent cost (much like
43           an accountant uses last-in-first-out --LIFO---for inventory valuation).
44


     Note: Bold faced type in answers indicates trade secret material. Please refer to the assigned name when   30
            discussing.

                                                                                                                STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment B


     Q.      IS MR. POLLOCK'S ALLEGATION ON PAGE 19 STATING THAT RTP SALES
 2           COULD SUPPORT PRODUCTION INVESTMENT 123% HIGHER THAN
 3           GPC'S NET PRODUCTION PLANT CORRECT?
 4
 5   A.      No, and it contains numerous flaws. For one thing we have clearly shown previously that
 6           what Mr. Pollock is using as margin is not purely production plant margin. Mr. Pollock's
 7           testimony calculated "margin" as the difference between the total selling price and the
 8           associated Fuel Cost Rate (FCR). However, a margin should be calculated as the
 9           difference between the selling price and the costs of production. His approach ignores
10           several key issues: (1) FCR recovers the total average fuel costs for all of the energy
11           supplied by Georgia Power Company. The correct method of calculating RTP margin
12           would include subtracting marginal fuel and purchase power costs from RTP revenues.
13           (2) Subtracting certain transmission costs associated with RTP. (3) Subtracting certain
14           generation reliability costs associated with RTP. (4) Subtracting risk cost associated with
15           RTP. In addition, there are clean air, commitment costs, additional distribution plant, and
16           incremental overheads that "margin" must cover.
17
18           The RTP rate was designed to provide customers with the benefits of marginal pricing
19           while capturing marginal cost associated with serving RTP loads. It is incorrect to
20           assume that fuel is the only marginal cost associated with RTP load and it also incorrect
21           to assume that RTP fuel costs are equal to average fuel costs for the entire company.
22
23           Second, even if you performed the computation correctly, you certainly could not
24           compare this marginal cost margin to GPC's "net production plant, which has a book
25           value of about $340 per kW ... ". Marginal cost are distinctly different from net plant
26           book value, just like replacement cost are very different from vintage cost. The SES
27           could certainly not replace its production plant today at $340 per kW. Finally, if Mr.
28           Pollock's idea here is to compare a "margin contribution" from RTP after removing the
29           FCR, even if one thought this were a reasonable exercise, the fact is that CT investment
30           cost is recovered through the outage cost component. This so-called lambda contribution
31           above FCR is not necessary for recovery of CT cost per kW. Therefore, one should
32           remove CT cost from the $340 per kW before making a comparison using this line of
33           reasoning.
34
35   Q.      PLEASE EXPAND ON MR. POLLOCK'S DEFINITION OF LAMBDA AS
36           EXCLUDING PURCHASE POWER.
37
38   A.      His definition applies to unit lambda only, not to system lambda. Lambda, as it applies to
39           individual, fuel fired generating units per the IIC, includes:
40                           Unit Incremental Heat Rate at output P (b + 2cP)
41                           Marginal Fuel Cost (FC)
42                           Incremental emissions cost (EC, excluded from GPC RTP lambda)
43                           Fuel Handling Cost (FH)
44                           Variable Operating and Maintenance Cost (VOM)
45                           Transmission Penalty Factor (TPF)
46

basis these costs also flow 18 through the FCR The FCR is a cost pass through mechanism with no profit feature All 19 retail customers of GPC whether residential commercial or RTP customers have the 20 same fuel cost responsibility broken down into 3 distinct voltage levels of service This 21 average costing mechanism has been deemed a fair way by this Commission for the strict 22 collection of fuel cost and related purchase power expenses 23 24 With most GPC tariffs there is a separate distinct FCR component This component is 25 produced by multiplying the customer s monthly kWh consumption times the current 26 applicable FCR rate This procedure is also performed on the standard bill CBL portion 27 of an RTP customer since a base rate is applied to the CBL However with the 28 incremental RTP portion of the bill there is already a component lambda in the RTP 29 price which collects for several costs one of which is fuel So to prevent double 30 recovery the FCR rate does not show up as  1       (2)    The changes proposed by GTMA and GIG to the RTP pricing structure would not

 6       (3)    GPC has provided no persuasive evidence to justify retaining the adders. In

                                          1. RTP Cost Basis


     Q   GPC WITNESSES STATE ON PAGE 7 THAT THE INTENT OF RTP IS AND ALWAYS

 2       HAS BEEN TO REVEAL THE MARGINAL COST OF MAKING MARGINAL CHANGES

 3       IN LOAD. DO YOU CONCUR WITH THIS STATEMENT?

 4   A   Yes, I do. It is important to note that RTP was designed to recover GPC's marginal cost

 5       of producing and delivering electricity. These marginal costs include:

 6       •      Incremental generation costs (i.e., fuel and variable operation and maintenance
 7              expense);

 8       •       Incremental transmission costs;

 9       •       Incremental generation capacity costs related to maintaining reliability; and

10       •       Line losses.

11       RTP was not designed to recover embedded transmission costs, distribution costs and

12       other overhead costs. This is because changes in electricity consumption do not directly

13       result in corresponding changes in these embedded costs.


14   Q   IF RTP DOES NOT RECOVER EMBEDDED TRANSMISSION, DISTRIBUTION AND

15       OVERHEAD COSTS, WHERE ARE THESE COSTS RECOVERED?

16   A   These costs are recovered in the customer baseline (CBL) portion of an RTP customer's

17       service. The CBL represents a customer's historical load that GPC was serving prior to

18       the inception of RTP service. The CBL portion of this service is priced under one of the

19       Company's standard embedded cost rates. Therefore, all of the Company's embedded

20       costs that are related to a customer's CBL are recovered in the CBL portion of RTP

21       customers' electricity costs.


                                                                               1. RTP Cost Basis

                                         BRUBAKER & AsSOCIATES, INC.


                                                                                                    II II         11

                                                                                                         STF-JKA-3-9 Attachment D


                                                                                                Jeffry Pollock
                                                                                          Rebuttal Testimony
                                                                                                      Page4

      Q        IS THIS SEPARATION OF COST RECOVERY BETWEEN THE CBL AND RTP
 2             COMPONENTS GENERALLY ACCEPTED IN THE INDUSTRY?
 3    A       Yes. This practice is described in a study conducted for the Electric Power Research

 4             Institute (EPRI). Specifically, the EPRI study states that:

 5                       MThe revenues from a customer can be thought of as covering two kinds
 6                       of costs: marginal costs and overhead costs. Marginal costs are those
 7                       that are clearly assignable to the customer's usage. They represent the
 8                       additional costs that the utility has to incur in order to serve the customer
 9                       - or the cost that the utility would save if the customer reduced usage to
10                       zero. For our purposes in this guidebook, overhead costs are all those
11                       costs that are not marginal costs. Under RTP service, the customer pays
12                       for marginal costs in the hourly energy charges. The methods of payment
13                       for overhead costs depend upon whether the RTP structure is one- or
14                       two-part. Under a one-part structure, overhead is collected in the adder
15                       or multiplier that is applied at marginal cost to arrive at the hourly price.
16                       In the two-part structure, overhead is collected through the access fee. nl


17   Q        DOES GPC HAVE A ONE-PART OR TWO-PART RTP STRUCTURE?

18   A        GPC's RTP tariffs have a two-part structure. This means that overhead is collected in

19            the CBL portion of the bill.


20   Q        BASED ON THIS EXPLANATION, IS IT VALID TO COMPARE MARGINAL COST

21            AND EMBEDDED COST AS SHOWN IN EXHIBIT_ (HK0-12)?

22   A        No. This comparison is invalid because RTP was not designed to recover the same

23            types of costs as GPC's standard embedded cost tariffs. Further, comparisons of this

24            type fail to recognize the substantial price risks borne by RTP customers.           This risk

25            differential can be seen in Exhibit _ _ (HK0-2). The Exhibit clearly shows that two-part

26            RTP service poses virtually no cost risk on the seller, meaning that all of the risk is borne

27            by the buyer, or customer. This is in contrast to other standard pricing options in which

28           the seller appropriately bears most of the cost risk.

              Christensen Associates, MReal Time Pricing Quick Start Guide," prepared for EPRI, Final Report,
     dated August 1995, Page xxi. (emphasis added). In GPC's case, the access fee is the same as the CBL
     or Standard Bill.

     Q       WHAT IS THE IMPLICATION OF THE GREATER ,RISK BORNE BY RTP

 2           CUSTOMERS?

 3   A       The greater the risk borne by the customer, the lower the price that the customer should

 4           be required to pay for electricity. RTP service requires the customers to bear all of the

 5           price risk. Therefore, RTP should be the least costly service provided by GPC on a per

 6           kWh basis, all other things being equal.

                                   2. RTP Pricing Structure


     Q   GPC WITNESSES HAVE ASSERTED THAT REMOVING PURCHASED POWER

 2       FROM LAMBDA IN SETTING THE RTP PRICE WOULD NO LONGER MAKE RTP A

 3       MARGINAL COST RATE. DO YOU CONCUR?

 4   A   No. This is an overstatement. Incremental generation costs determine real time prices

 5       during the vast majority of hours.    Expensive purchases are only required when the

 6       Company does not have sufficient generation to meet territorial loads.         As it is the

 7       Company's objective to always have sufficient resources to satisfy customers' needs for

 8       reliable low cost service, the instances where expensive power purchases set the real

 9       time price should be the exception and not the rule. Trends would indicate the opposite.

10              Limiting the system lambda to include only incremental generation cost would

11       continue to send marginal cost-based price signals to customers.          This is because

12       incremental generation costs can range from 1.2¢ to as high as 7.5¢ per kWh. As low-

13       cost base load energy is exhausted and new resources are added that are fueled with

14       more expensive natural gas, these higher costs will immediately be reflected in the

15       hourly real time prices. This is consistent with sending marginal cost price signals.


16   Q   DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCERNS ABOUT WHETHER THE COMPANY WILL HAVE

17       SUFFICIENT GENERATION TO SATISFY CUSTOMERS' NEEDS?

18   A   Yes. The Company mentions that new capacity additions will help to reduce real time

20       projected load growth. As I demonstrated in Exhibit _       (JP-3) attached to my Direct

21       Testimony, the projected reserve margins in the Southern Subregion are currently well

22       below a 15% planning reserve. This means that the utilities must add more resources

23       than projected load growth in order to restore a 15% reserve margin.

     Q       WOULD LAMBDA AVERAGING ALSO SEND MARGINAL COST PRICE SIGNALS?

 2   A       Yes. Lambda averaging is just another way of quantifying marginal cost. As I stated in

 3           my Direct Testimony, there is no universally accepted definition of system lambda.

 4           Some utilities, like GPC, define system lambda as the cost of the next kWh generated.

 5          Other utilities use lambda averaging. Thus, the issue is not which definition reflects

 6          marginal cost because both GPC's lambdas and lambda averaging are marginal cost-

 7          based.

 8                   The real Issue is which definition of lambda best tracks the actual cost to provide

 9          RTP service. As I demonstrated in my Direct Testimony, lambda averaging more closely

1O          reflects the actual incremental cost to serve RTP loads. This is precisely the reason why

11          the Commission should adopt full lambda averaging in this proceeding.

     Q   DO THE COMPANY'S CONCERNS ABOUT ADDITIONAL DISTRIBUTION AND

 2       RELATED OVERHEAD COSTS APPLY TO ALL RTP CUSTOMERS?

 3   A   No. Many RTP customers take service directly from the transmission system. In fact,

 4       the larger GIG and GTMA members that take service on RTP-HA are almost entirely at

 5       transmission voltage. GPC does not invest in distribution equipment to serve the needs

 6       of transmission-level customers. Thus, even if the Company's concerns were valid, it

 7       would not justify collecting the same revenues from all RTP customers because many of

 8       these customers - especially larger GIG and GTMA members - are served directly at

 9       the transmission level.


10   Q   ARE UNIT COMMITMENT COSTS ONLY INCURRED TO SERVE RTP CUSTOMERS?

11   A   No. These costs are incurred whenever the Company must start-up a generating unit in

12       anticipation of serving loads that are expected to occur the next day. Typically, this

13       occurs during off-peak hours. Unit commitments are generally required because of time-

14       of-clay variations in load.   Day-time loads are typically much higher than night-time

15       loads.    Adequate generation must be available to meet these day-time loads.      The

16       problem is that many generators cannot be turned on and turned off to instantly respond

17       to changes in load. Units must be committed ahead of time (usually on the previous day

18       or night) to meet projected daily demands.

19                Thus, unit commitment costs are a system-wide cost. They cannot be solely

20       attributed to RTP customers.       However, if any attempt were made to allocate unit

21       commitment costs to specific customers, then they should be allocated relative to

22       on-peak usage because on-peak usage causes unit commitment costs to be incurred.

     Q   WOULD ELIMINATING THE ADDERS VIOLATE THE EARNINGS SHARING

 2       PROVISION OF THE ACCOUNTING ORDER?

 3   A   No. It will have no impact on the sharing of earnings during calendar year 1999 since

 4       the results of this case will not be applied retroactively.   As I stated in my Direct

 5       Testimony, GPC's future earnings will depend on a variety of factors, including how well

 6       the Company manages its operating expenses. Absent a severe economic reversal, a

 7       resurgence of inflation or other unknown event, there is every reason to believe that,

 8       based on past performance, the Company's earnings will continue to generate refunds

 9       for all customers.


10   Q   WOULD      ELIMINATING      THE      ADDER       ADVERSELY    AFFECT      THE    PRICE

11       RESPONSIVENESS OF RTP?

12   A   No. Price responsiveness is a function of the hourly marginal cost. The adder is not a
13       marginal cost associated with generation, it is simply a constant amount added to the

14       hourly real time price. This is in contrast to the other RTP components that vary each

15       hour depending on system operating conditions. Changes in these components, which

16       result in corresponding changes in hourly real time prices, convey the appropriate price

17       signals and encourage customers to respond accordingly. The adder, unlike the other

18       RTP cost components, is nothing more than pure profit to GPC. GPC does not need

19       this additional profit to fully recover embedded generation cost from RTP customers.

                                  4. Revenue Comparisons


     Q   HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE 1998 INDUSTRIAL PRICE PER kWh COMPARISONS

 2       PROVIDED WITH THE GPC TESTIMONY?

 3   A   Yes. GPC's comparisons are shown in Exhibit __ (HK0-8).


 4   Q   ARE THE COMPARISONS SHOWN IN THIS EXHIBIT A VALID ANALYSIS?

 5   A   No. First, the Exhibit is mislabeled. Contrary to the label, these comparisons do not

 6       represent actual prices paid by individual customers. This is because the numbers were

 7       derived by dividing average revenues paid by industrial customers by the total kWh sold

 8       to industrial customers in 1998. Actual price comparisons were provided in Exhibit __

 9       (JP-1) attached to my Direct Testimony.

10              Second, GPC made an error in the average revenue for Duke Power Company

11       South Carolina. The correct number is 3.59¢, not 4.59¢.

12              The Exhibit also gives the mistaken impression that Savannah Electric's

13       industrial rates are cheaper than Georgia Power's, when the opposite is true. It just so

14       happens that Savannah's industrial customers are six-times larger than GPC's average

15       industrial customer. As explained later, it is much less costly to serve larger customers

16       on a per kWh basis. When more energy is sold at a lower price, the result is to lower the

17       average revenue per kWh for the entire class. Consider the following example:


                                                          UtlliwA             Utillw B
                                                       Sales        Price   Sales   Price

                       Rate 1                            50         3.00¢   450     3.25¢

                       Rate2                             150        4.00¢    50     4.50¢

                       Average Revenue per kWh                      3.75¢           3.37¢

         As can be seen, Utility B has higher prices than Utility A. 'However, because Utility B
 2       sells more energy at a lower rate (Rate 1}, its average revenue per kWh is lower than

 3       Utility A. This example demonstrates how average revenue per kWh comparisons can

 4       be misleading.


 5   Q   WHY ELSE ARE GPC'S COMPARISONS MISLEADING?

 6   A   Including GIG and GTMA average cost per kWh information is a classic apples and

 7       oranges comparison. It is simply wrong to compare a select group of GPC's customers

 8       to the average per kWh revenues paid by all industrial customers served by other

 9       southeastern electric utilities.

1o               Notwithstanding the apples and oranges nature of the per kWh comparisons,

11       GPC selectively omitted Kentucky Power Company, TVA and several other low-cost

12       utilities. It is no coincidence that the average revenues per kWh derived from industrial

13       sales by the utilities that GPC selectively omitted are below the amounts shown for GIG

14       and GTMA members. The complete listing for all Southeastern utilities is provided in

15       Exhibit_ (JP-12). These are the same utilities used in the Mapples-to-apples· price

16       comparisons shown in Exhibit __ (JP-1}, page 3.

17              Finally, average revenue per kWh comparisons mask fundamental differences in

18       the usage and other characteristics that determine the per kWh cost of providing service.


19   Q   DOES GPC PRESENT ANY VALID REASON FOR EXCLUDING TVA FROM ITS

20       REVENUE COMPARISONS?

21   A   No. TVA is a major competitor to GPC. This conclusion is not altered by the fact that

22       TVA has a different financial and tax structure than GPC.

     Q   CAN ANY LEGITIMATE CONCLUSIONS BE DRAWN BY COMPARING THE GIG

 2       AND GTMA AVERAGE REVENUES PER kWh WITH THE CORRESPONDING

 3       AVERAGE INDUSTRIAL REVENUES OF CUSTOMERS SERVED BY OTHER

 4       UTILITIES?

 5   A   No. By their very nature, averages mean that some customers pay more per kWh for

 6       service, while other customers pay less. Closer examination of the average revenues

 7       per kWh charged by other utilities to selected industrial customers reveals that GIG and

 8       GTMA members are not getting the best deal, contrary to the false impression created

 9       by GPC's Exhibit.

10              For example, average revenues per kWh sold to Rate HLF customers served by

11       Alabama Power Company (GPC's affiliate) are only 3.01¢ per kWh.           Another GPC

12       affiliate, Mississippi Power Company, recovers only 2.56¢ per kWh from its Rate LPO

13       industrial customers. Louisville Gas and Electric, which was omitted from GPC's Exhibit,

14       recovers 3.10¢ per kWh from its special contract customers and only 3.50¢ per kWh

15       from its large industrial time-of-day customers.     Although some industrial rates are

16       higher than the examples shown above, it is clear that GPC is not the lowest cost

17       supplier in the Southeast to customers like GIG and GTMA members.


18   Q   DO GPC'S COMPARISONS PRESENT A COMPLETE PICTURE OF CURRENT RATE

19       AND COST RELATIONSHIPS?

20   A   No.   The examples presented earlier demonstrate the fallacy of comparing average

21       revenues between selected customer groups and broad industrial class averages. What

22       is missing from GPC's analysis is evidence that compares the actual cost of providing

23       service to industrial customers similar to individual GIG and GTMA members.

     Q    WHAT WOULD A COST STUDY SHOW?

 2   A   A cost study would show that it is common practice to charge lower rates for customers

 3       that operate at a higher load factor, take service at a higher delivery voltage, consume

 4       more electricity per meter, who are willing to either curtail service or assume price risk

 5       and whose load shape is more off-peak in nature.


 6   Q   WHAT IS LOAD FACTOR?

 7   A   Load factor is a measure of how customers use the capacity that they impose on the

 8       utility.   A high load factor customer uses capacity steadily around the clock and

 9       throughout the year. A lower load factor means that electricity is used more intensively

10       during certain times of the year (e.g., the hot summer months for air conditioning load).

11       In general, the higher the load factor, the lower the cost to serve per kWh.


12   Q   HOW DOES DELIVERY VOLTAGE AFFECT AVERAGE REVENUES PER kWh?

13   A   Customers that take service at a higher voltage level are less costly to serve for two

14       reasons.    First, GPC does not have to incur lower voltage distribution costs to serve

15       transmission-level customers.     Nor does GPC incur as many losses to serve a

16       transmission-level customer. With less investment and lower losses, service provided at

17       transmission voltage is less costly on a per kWh basis.


18   Q   HOW DOES SIZE AFFECT THE PER kWh COST TO SERVE?

19   A   Larger customers require more expensive metering, and billing and customer accounting

20       costs are generally higher per location than for smaller customers.       However, these

21       costs are not proportional to the amount of kWh consumption. Thus, customer-related

22       costs to serve larger customers are lower on a per kWh basis.

     Q   IS THERE EVIDENCE THAT GEORGIA POWER'S INDUSTRIAL CUSTOMERS HAVE
 2       DIFFERENT COST CHARACTERISTICS?

 3   A   Yes. Exhibit __ (JP-13) is a summary of the cost characteristics for GPC's industrial

 4       class.    It shows demand, energy, load factor, number of customers and average

 5       consumption (size) separated by delivery voltage.

 6                The Exhibit demonstrates that industrial customers are served at a wide range of

 7       delivery voltages:    from 115 kV transmission lines to distribution line transformers.

 8       There are also differences in load factor as a function of delivery voltage. Similarly,

 9       larger customers tend to be served at the higher voltages (e.g., transmission lines and

10       substations).   Finally, although the majority of the industrial load is served at higher

11       voltage, the vast majority of the industrial customers are served at distribution voltage.

12       (All residential and most commercial customers are also served at this distribution level.)

13                These different characteristics suggest that it is inappropriate to compare

14       average industrial revenues on a per kWh basis. Such comparisons must also consider

15       differences in the characteristics that result in differences in the actual cost to serve per

16       kWh.


17   Q   DO AVERAGE REVENUE PER kWh COMPARISONS BETWEEN BROADLY

18       DEFINED CLASSES REFLECT DIFFERENCES BETWEEN FIRM AND NONFIRM

19       SERVICE?
20   A   No.    Nonfirm or interruptible customers        take a lower quality of service than firm

21       customers. This is because the utility can require nonfirm customers to curtail their

22       service so that sufficient capacity is available to enable the utility to continue meeting the

23       needs of its firm customers.

     Q   IS NONFIRM SERVICE LESS COSTLY THAN FIRM SERVICE?

 2   A   Yes.


 3   Q   DO AVERAGE REVENUE PER kWh COMPARISONS REVEAL DIFFERENCES IN

 4       PRICE RISK?

 5   A   No. These comparisons do not differentiate between standard embedded tariffs and

 6       real time pricing, which places customers entirely at risk for changes in system operating

 7       conditions and costs.


 8   Q   DO RTP CUSTOMERS THAT HAVE DIFFERENT LOAD SHAPES PAY THE SAME

 9       AVERAGE REVENUES PER RTP kWh SOLD?

10   A   No. These differences are illustrated in GPC's Exhibit __ (HK0-16). For example,

11       Customer X, which has a completely flat load shape, would pay an average RTP price of

12       3.09¢ per kWh. Customer Y, whose load shape is more summer peaking, would pay

13       3.25¢, which is a higher average price per kWh than Customer X.                 Similarly,

14       Customer Z, who has a more off-peak load shape, would pay only 2.95¢ for RTP

15       service, which is a lower average price than either Customer's X and Y pay.


16   Q   WOULD THESE CHARACTERISTICS EXPLAIN IN LARGE PART WHY GIG AND

17       GTMA CUSTOMERS PAY LESS PER kWh THAN DO OTHER GEORGIA POWER
18       INDUSTRIAL CUSTOMERS?

19   A   Yes. Both the GIG and GTMA customers are among the largest loads served by GPC.

20       This means that average customer costs per kWh are lower for these customers than for

21       smaller industrial loads. Many GIG and GTMA customers take service at higher delivery

22       voltages. This means that GPC incurs less investment and lower losses to serve these

23       customers, resulting in a lower average cost per kWh. Most GIG and GTMA members

         normally operate either multiple shifts or around the clock. ·Thus, they generally have

 2       higher load factors than most industrial customers. This further reduces the average

 3       cost per kWh. Several of the larger members take interruptible service. Interruptible

 4       service is less costly than firm service on a per kWh basis. Finally, many GIG and

 5       GTMA members take real time pricing. RTP is more risky than standard service. This

 6       additional risk, coupled with the generally more off-peak load shapes of these

instantly respond 17 to changes in load Units must be committed ahead of time usually on the previous day 18 or night to meet projected daily demands 19 Thus unit commitment costs are a system wide cost They cannot be solely 20 attributed to RTP customers However if any attempt were made to allocate unit 21 commitment costs to specific customers then they should be allocated relative to 22 on
